problems.title: Machine-check the universality of Rule 110
problems.question: Can Cook's proof that elementary cellular automaton Rule 110 is computationally universal be formalized and checked in Lean 4 with no `sorry` and no added axioms?
problems.known_state: Cook (2004) proved universality by emulating cyclic tag systems with glider collisions; Neary and Woods (2006) sharpened the emulation to polynomial time. Neither proof has been machine-checked. The repo records the claim as inconclusive (wolfram2002-ch11-14) because reproduction tests can only exercise the construction, not verify it.
acceptance_criteria: A Lean 4 module whose main theorem states that for every cyclic tag system and input there is an initial configuration of Rule 110 whose evolution encodes the computation, compiled with no sorry and only Lean's standard axioms.
The glider catalog, collision table and the periodic background are each a checked lemma rather than an assumption.
falsifiers: A gap in the collision table that cannot be closed (a required collision that does not behave as Cook's table says), which would also be a finding against the published proof.
problems.data_access: No data needed; Rule 110 is fully specified. Cook's glider tables are in the open-access Complex Systems paper.

related_claims.label: Elementary cellular automaton rule 110 is universal
A 2-state 5-color Turing machine is universal via rule 110
Universal computation is possible in systems with one-sentence rules

approaches.title: Modular Lean proof of Cook's construction via a light-cone splicing lemma
approaches.method: Formalize Rule 110 as a map on configurations ℤ → Bool and prove Cook's emulation of cyclic tag systems (CTS) as a stack of independent layers. The load-bearing general lemma is locality (light-cone splicing): the restriction of step^[t] x to the interval [a+t, b−t] depends only on x restricted to [a, b]. With it, any finite pattern embedded in the periodic ether can be checked on a finite window by kernel computation (`decide` or `rfl` on List Bool, never `native_decide`), and the result transfers to the infinite configuration. Layers: (1) the ether is spacetime-periodic: it returns to a spatial shift of itself after its temporal period (Cook gives horizontal period 14 and vertical period 7); (2) each glider Cook uses (A through H and the variants in his construction) is a finite word that, spliced into ether, reappears translated after its period; (3) each collision in Cook's table, at each phase and offset the construction uses, produces the stated outgoing gliders, checked on a finite window; (4) a glider calculus: an abstract configuration (a list of glider type, phase and gap triples), an interpretation map into Rule 110 configurations, and a simulation theorem saying that for gaps above a stated threshold the CA evolution realizes the abstract collision rules; (5) Cook's encoding of CTS tape, appendants and the periodic right-hand program stream, with a theorem that one CTS step corresponds to a bounded number of abstract collision rounds.
steps: Define `rule110`, `step`, shift, and prove the light-cone splicing lemma by induction on t.
Encode the ether word and prove its spacetime periodicity on a finite window; lift to ℤ with the splicing lemma.
Transcribe Cook's glider catalogue and collision table from the open-access Complex Systems paper into Lean data; prove each entry by bounded kernel computation.
Define the abstract glider-list semantics and prove the simulation theorem for well-separated configurations.
Define cyclic tag systems in Lean and Cook's encoding; prove the one-step correspondence and the main theorem by induction on CTS steps.
Check `#print axioms` lists only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound; write a report in the format of the Thompson Lean reports.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean 4 module whose main theorem states: for every cyclic tag system and input word there is an initial Rule 110 configuration (ether plus a finite perturbation on the left and a periodic glider stream on the right) and a decoding map such that the CA evolution encodes every CTS step. It must compile with no sorry and only the three standard axioms, with every glider and collision fact a proved lemma.
approaches.failure_signature: A collision required by the encoding that the kernel check refutes at the phase or gap the construction needs (a gap in Cook's table, itself a publishable finding), or kernel computations on the required windows that are too large to complete without native_decide, forcing the project to stall at layer 3.
approaches.missing: Proof-engineering volume rather than new mathematics: Cook's construction has many glider spacings and timing constraints, and kernel-only evaluation of large windows may be slow. A month is likely enough for layers 1 to 3, not the full chain.

approaches.title: Independent exhaustive audit of Cook's glider and collision table
approaches.method: Before or alongside formalization, re-derive from scratch every fact Cook's construction depends on, using code written without reference to Cook's tables except for the final comparison. Enumerate all gliders on the ether background up to period 200 and width 100 using de Bruijn-diagram search for spacetime-periodic patterns. For every ordered pair of gliders used by the construction, simulate the collision at every relative phase and every integer gap in the range the construction allows, and record the outgoing glider multiset with phases. Then run the full construction for small cyclic tag systems (including Cook's worked example and randomly generated CTS with up to 6 appendants of length up to 6) for at least 10^7 generations with bit-parallel simulation, and decode the CTS tape from the glider stream at each emulated step, comparing with a direct CTS interpreter.
steps: Implement a bit-sliced Rule 110 simulator and a de Bruijn-diagram glider finder; verify against the published list of Rule 110 gliders.
Produce a machine-readable collision table (JSON) over all phases and gaps used by the construction, with SHA-256 of the generating code and output.
Diff the table against a transcription of Cook's table; classify every discrepancy as transcription error, phase-convention difference or genuine mismatch.
Run end-to-end emulations of at least 100 random CTS and compare decoded tapes step by step with a reference interpreter.
approaches.decisive_result: Either a complete match (every collision the construction needs behaves as stated at every allowed gap, and all end-to-end emulations decode correctly for 10^7 generations), which hands layer 3 of a formal proof a verified target, or a specific (glider pair, phase, gap) triple whose outcome differs from Cook's table and breaks an emulation.
approaches.failure_signature: The audit cannot settle universality either way by itself; it fails as an approach if the gap ranges the construction needs cannot be extracted unambiguously from the paper, so the audit checks a reconstruction rather than Cook's proof.

approaches.title: Verified certificate checker: reduce the proof to a finite spacetime tile set
approaches.method: Instead of proving Cook's construction lemma by lemma, prove once in Lean that a small checker is sound, and let external search produce the certificate. The spacetime diagram of Cook's construction for an arbitrary CTS is assembled from finitely many rectangular spacetime tiles (ether blocks, glider segments, collision blocks), and the program side is periodic while the data side varies only through which tiles are chosen. Define in Lean a certificate as a finite tile set with edge labels (boundary words) plus a context-free or regular grammar describing admissible tile arrangements for any CTS. The checker verifies (a) each tile is a valid Rule 110 spacetime patch, by kernel computation, (b) adjacent tiles agree on shared boundary words, (c) the grammar generates, for each CTS step, an arrangement whose decoded output equals the CTS successor. Soundness theorem: if the checker accepts, the universality statement holds. This fails differently from approach 1: the human-proof burden shrinks to the soundness lemma and the grammar semantics, while the computational burden moves to certificate generation outside Lean.
steps: Specify tiles, boundary words and the arrangement grammar in Lean; prove the soundness theorem using the light-cone splicing lemma.
Write an external generator that runs the construction on many CTS, cuts the spacetime diagram into tiles, deduplicates them and infers the arrangement grammar.
Run the checker inside Lean by kernel reduction on the certificate; iterate on tile size if kernel cost is prohibitive.
Prove the grammar-to-CTS correspondence by induction on CTS steps.
approaches.decisive_result: Lean accepts the certificate, and the soundness theorem plus the checker run yields the universality theorem with only standard axioms. A secondary artifact is the tile count, a compact measure of the construction's complexity.
approaches.failure_signature: The tile decomposition does not close: arrangements depend on unbounded gap values in a way no regular or context-free grammar captures, or the tile set needed exceeds what kernel reduction can check in reasonable time.
approaches.missing: No existing tile-level description of Cook's construction; the grammar-inference step is research.

approaches.title: Refinement proof from cyclic tag systems to Rule 110
approaches.method: Define finite Rule 110 windows with a periodic ether outside, cyclic tag systems, and a decoding relation in Lean 4. Prove a one-step simulation theorem by decomposing each compiled tag step into a finite sequence of glider phases; discharge each collision lemma with a kernel-evaluated finite trace and compose them by induction on tag-system runs.
steps: Formalize Rule 110 evolution on integers and prove locality and light-cone lemmas.
Encode Cook's ether phases, gliders and compiler from cyclic tag words.
Generate every required collision trace and prove its decoded precondition and postcondition by decide.
Prove phase synchronization, noninterference and the global simulation theorem without sorry.
approaches.decisive_result: A compiling Lean module whose theorem maps every finite cyclic-tag execution of length k to a Rule 110 execution decoding the same k transitions, with all collision and ether lemmas proved and only standard axioms.
approaches.failure_signature: A required compiler collision has no finite spacetime trace with Cook's advertised phase and separation constraints, or collision lemmas cannot be composed because debris enters another light cone.
approaches.missing: A machine-readable transcription of Cook's complete glider phase table and substantial Lean proof engineering.

approaches.title: Certified collision-table reconstruction
approaches.method: Independently reconstruct Cook's construction before formalizing it. Enumerate all ether-relative glider phases and pair/triple collisions inside exact light cones, canonicalize traces modulo translation and ether period, and search for a closed macro-transition system implementing the cyclic tag productions. Emit proof certificates containing initial words, horizons and decoded products for Lean replay.
steps: Enumerate minimal periodic-ether defects up to width 80 and classify velocities over 500 steps.
Enumerate phase-separated collisions up to distance 400 and retain stable products.
Model compilation as a constraint problem over collision phases and spacings.
Replay every selected certificate in Lean and compare the reconstructed table with the published construction.
approaches.decisive_result: A closed, independently generated set of certified macro-transitions sufficient for both cyclic-tag productions and all routing operations, with every trace replayed by Lean.
approaches.failure_signature: Exhaustive bounded search finds that at least one required macro-transition has no phase-consistent realization within the stated bounds, leaving no complete emulation certificate.
approaches.missing: Completeness beyond finite phase and spacing bounds would still require a mathematical argument.

approaches.title: Kernel-check Cook's ether, gliders and collision table
approaches.method: In the repo's Lean 4.35.0 and Mathlib 4.35.0, encode Rule 110 as the Boolean function on (Bool × Bool × Bool) given by Wolfram's 8-bit table number 110. Do not use the formula left XOR (center OR right); that formula is Rule 30. Transcribe the periodic background word and every glider word from Cook 2004, without rewriting them. Prove the background is invariant under the spacetime shift Cook states. For each published collision, evolve the finite word with a pure Lean function and prove equality to Cook's product word by kernel reduction (rfl or decide on a Bool), never native_decide, sorry, or an extra axiom. Split any evolution the kernel cannot reduce in one pass into blocks of a few hundred steps with an intermediate word that is itself a lemma. The glider catalog, the background and the collision table are separate lemmas, as the acceptance criteria require.
steps: Define rule110 : Bool × Bool × Bool → Bool from the 8-bit table and prove it matches Wolfram number 110.
Transcribe Cook's periodic background and prove the invariance he claims.
Transcribe each glider as a finite word on that background.
Discharge each collision lemma by blocked kernel reduction of the pure step function.
Record #print axioms output and reject the module if any axiom other than propext, Classical.choice or Quot.sound appears.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean module, with no sorry, whose lemmas are exactly Cook's background, glider catalog and collision table, each proved by reduction of the cellular-automaton step.
approaches.failure_signature: Any transcribed collision evolves to a word different from Cook's table, or a collision is too long for blocked kernel reduction and no alternative proof is found. A mismatched collision is also evidence against the published table.
approaches.missing: Nothing external. The obstacle is proof size: Cook's table is a long finite case analysis, and Lean's kernel may force very small blocks.

approaches.title: Formalize cyclic-tag universality before any glider
approaches.method: Separate the computability half of Cook's argument from the cellular-automaton half, so a bug in a glider collision cannot hide inside a tag-system lemma. Define a cyclic tag system as a finite list of appendants, a binary work string, and the rotation that appends the next word and deletes the front bit. Formalize the Cocke–Minsky simulation of a binary Turing machine by a 2-tag system, then Cook's simulation of a 2-tag system by a cyclic tag system. The main theorem is: for every Turing machine and input there is a cyclic tag system and an encoding of the input such that the tag system halts if and only if the machine does, with an explicit bound on the number of tag steps per machine step. Do not mention Rule 110 in this module. Hypotheses that Cook leaves informal (the precise halting convention, the treatment of the empty appendant) stay as named hypotheses rather than as sorry.
steps: Define Turing machines, 2-tag systems and cyclic tag systems with explicit halting.
Formalize the Cocke–Minsky encoding and prove one-step correspondence.
Formalize Cook's tag-to-cyclic-tag encoding and prove one-step correspondence.
Compose the two simulations and extract the overhead bound.
Audit axioms. Leave Rule 110 out of the imports.
approaches.decisive_result: A no-sorry theorem that cyclic tag systems simulate every Turing machine, with the step overhead as a proved bound.
approaches.failure_signature: A one-step correspondence fails on a finite witness (a tag system whose encoded run disagrees with the machine), or the halting convention cannot be stated without an extra axiom.

approaches.title: Compose glider lemmas into the emulation theorem
approaches.method: Assuming the collision lemmas and the cyclic-tag theorem as already checked modules, formalize Cook's compiler: a function from a cyclic tag system and a finite input to a finite set of gliders on the background. The theorem is a lockstep bisimulation. Each tag step is a fixed finite sequence of the checked collisions, and the encoding of the work string is an invariant of that sequence. Prefer the Neary–Woods polynomial-overhead presentation where it cites the same gliders, and prove the polynomial bound as a separate lemma rather than hiding it in the invariant. This module is forbidden to re-verify collisions by simulation; it may only apply the lemmas from the catalog. That split is what makes a failure here different from a failure in the table.
steps: Define the compiler from cyclic tag systems to Rule 110 configurations using only named gliders.
State the representation invariant (work string, phase, and head glider).
Prove that each tag operation is a composition of catalogued collisions.
Prove the overhead bound, polynomial if the Neary–Woods schedule is the one formalized.
Compose with cyclic-tag universality to obtain the Rule 110 universality theorem and audit axioms.
approaches.decisive_result: A no-sorry theorem: for every cyclic tag system and input there is a Rule 110 configuration whose evolution encodes the computation, with gliders, collisions and background used only as prior lemmas.
approaches.failure_signature: The invariant fails on some tag operation even though every individual collision lemma is true, which means the compiler, not the table, is wrong. Partial gates with no bisimulation do not count.
approaches.missing: A month of agent time is unlikely to finish the bisimulation even after the collision lemmas exist. The missing piece is proof effort on the compiler invariant, not data or a new algorithm.

problems.title: Settle whether the (2,3) Turing machine is universal under a conventional definition
problems.question: Is Wolfram's 2-state 3-color Turing machine universal when the initial tape is required to be finite-support or eventually periodic, rather than the non-periodic infinite background used in Smith's prize proof?
problems.known_state: Smith's 2007 proof (published 2020) uses an infinite, non-periodic but computable initial tape, which several authors argue smuggles computation into the input. Standard small-universal-machine results (Neary and Woods) use blank or periodic backgrounds. Whether the (2,3) machine is universal under those definitions is open.
acceptance_criteria: Either a construction with a finite-support or eventually periodic initial tape that emulates a universal system, formalized in Lean 4, or a proof that no such construction exists (for example by showing the machine's behaviour on all eventually periodic tapes is decidable).
falsifiers: A decidability proof for eventually periodic inputs would refute universality under that definition.
problems.data_access: None needed; the machine is a 6-entry table.

related_claims.label: A 2-state 5-color Turing machine is universal via rule 110
No 2-state 2-color Turing machine can be universal
Exhaustive search of 2-state 2-color Turing machines finds three growth rates

approaches.title: Decidability route: regular invariants for the (2,3) machine on periodic backgrounds
approaches.method: Fix the decision problem first, since the (2,3) machine has no halt state: say 'does the head ever reach cell n' or 'does the tape ever contain word v within distance n of the origin', which is how Smith's emulation reads off computation. Restrict to eventually periodic tapes u^ω · w · v^ω. Use the bbchallenge decider family, adapted to non-halting machines: closed tape languages, finite-automata reduction (FAR) and translated-cycler detection. They search for a regular language L of configurations that contains the initial configuration, is closed under the step relation, and implies the property or its negation. Enumerate background pairs (u, v) with |u|, |v| ≤ 8 and windows |w| ≤ 12. If a uniform regular invariant family appears (for example, the machine reduces on every periodic background to a counter or pushdown system whose reachability is decidable), state and prove it in Lean as a decidability theorem. Systematic non-existence of small invariants, together with growth patterns resembling Smith's system 0, is evidence in the other direction and identifies the hardest background classes.
steps: Write the (2,3) rule table and a reference simulator; fix the observable (head-position or word-occurrence predicate) as the decision problem.
Port FAR and closed-tape-language deciders to non-halting predicates; validate on machines whose behaviour is known.
Run the enumeration over (u, w, v) and record which configurations admit regular invariants and with how many states.
If invariants follow a pattern, generalize by hand and formalize the decidability proof in Lean 4; otherwise publish the census of undecided cases.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean-checked theorem that the chosen predicate is decidable for all eventually periodic initial tapes, which refutes universality under that definition. Short of that, a census giving, for each background up to the bound, either a verified regular invariant or an explicit undecided configuration.
approaches.failure_signature: Many small backgrounds, including the blank one, resist all regular invariants up to large state counts, while showing irregular, nested head motion; the decidability route then probably cannot succeed.
approaches.missing: Mathematics beyond current automation if the machine is in fact universal on periodic backgrounds; adapting halting-oriented deciders to observables is new work.

approaches.title: Construction route: replace Smith's non-periodic tape with a periodic refuel gadget
approaches.method: Smith's proof is a chain: the (2,3) machine emulates system 0, which emulates a sequence of intermediate systems ending in a cyclic tag system, and the infinite non-periodic tape supplies the structures the chain consumes. Implement each layer as an executable specification and instrument the emulation to find exactly which layer consumes non-periodic structure, and what that structure is (for example, blocks whose lengths grow with the number of emulated steps). Then search for a replacement: a finite gadget on a periodic background that regenerates the consumed structure on demand. Neary and Woods' weakly universal small machines show this kind of periodic-background refuelling can work. The search runs over short periodic background words and finite gadgets (SAT or bounded model checking on the layer's step relation), with the requirement that the composed system still emulates the CTS.
steps: Implement Smith's systems 0 through 5 and the CTS layer as executable specs, with cross-checking simulation from a common CTS input.
Instrument the emulation to log the background symbols consumed per emulated CTS step and fit their growth law.
Formulate a SAT or bounded-model-checking search for a periodic background plus finite gadget that produces the consumed structure; run for background periods up to 40.
If a candidate is found, verify by long simulation and then formalize the composed emulation in Lean.
approaches.decisive_result: An explicit eventually periodic initial tape for which the (2,3) machine emulates a universal CTS, verified by simulation for at least 10^6 emulated steps and then proved in Lean. Even without success, the instrumented chain is a precise statement of what the non-periodic tape contributes, which the current literature lacks.
approaches.failure_signature: The consumed structure grows superlinearly in a way no finite gadget on a periodic background can produce (for example, its growth law implies the background must encode an unbounded counter), or the search exhausts all gadgets up to the size bound.
approaches.missing: Possibly a genuinely new idea; the search space for gadgets may be far too large.

approaches.title: Formalize Smith's proof and bound the computational power of its initial tape
approaches.method: Machine-check what is currently claimed, with the definitional issue stated exactly. Formalize in Lean 4 Smith's theorem: for every CTS there is a computable initial tape on which the (2,3) machine emulates it. Then prove a theorem about the tape's complexity, which is what the dispute is about. Candidate statements: the tape is generated by a fixed finite-state transducer from the CTS description and a fixed infinite word; it is a fixed morphic or automatic sequence modified by a finite prefix; or it is computable in linear time by a non-universal device. Each turns 'the encoding smuggles in computation' into a checkable claim. If the tape is automatic or morphic, the result places the (2,3) machine in a precisely named universality class between weak universality (periodic background) and Smith's notion.
steps: Formalize the (2,3) machine, CTS and Smith's intermediate systems in Lean; prove each emulation step.
Extract the explicit initial-tape generator from the proof and formalize it as a function.

Prove the generator lies in a named weak class (finite transducer over a fixed sequence, automatic sequence, or linear-time and non-universal), or show it cannot, by exhibiting an encoding step that requires unbounded computation.
Write a short mapping of the critics' objections onto the formal statements.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean module proving Smith's theorem together with a proved upper bound on the complexity of the required tape (for example 'the tape is k-automatic'). That settles the definitional dispute in the form 'universal under definition D', even though it leaves the periodic-background case open.
approaches.failure_signature: Formalization uncovers a gap in Smith's chain that cannot be closed, or the tape generator turns out to need unbounded computation in a way that makes every weak-class statement false.
approaches.missing: Smith's chain is long (about 40 pages of construction); the full formalization is likely beyond a month, though the tape-complexity analysis can be done on the informal proof first.

approaches.title: Search for periodic-background tag-system compilers
approaches.method: Treat an eventually periodic tape as left period, finite defect and right period. Enumerate periods up to 12 and defects up to 40 cells, then use symbolic execution and counterexample-guided synthesis to seek macro-configurations representing tag symbols and clock phases. Require compositional transitions, not isolated long transients, and certify candidates by exact simulation.
steps: Implement the six-entry machine and symmetry-reduced eventually periodic configurations.
Mine recurring spacetime motifs and infer finite-state macro-boundaries.
Synthesize encodings of a cyclic tag system with bounded phase jitter.
For any candidate, prove finite transition certificates and formulate an induction invariant in Lean.
approaches.decisive_result: A periodic-background compiler with exact certificates for both tag productions, erasure, appending and clock restoration, followed by a Lean simulation theorem.
approaches.failure_signature: No closed macro-transition set survives adversarial compositions of 10,000 random tag steps despite exhaustive periods and defect bounds; this falsifies the searched compiler family, not universality.
approaches.missing: No completeness theorem says universality must use a short periodic background or local tag encoding.

approaches.title: Decidability via bounded crossing sequences
approaches.method: Seek a negative result for eventually periodic tapes. Define crossing sequences at cell boundaries and prove that the 2-state control plus periodic tails forces either bounded crossing complexity or a pumpable translation cycle. A finite quotient of boundary state, tape color and tail phase would then decide halting and exclude conventional universality.
steps: Enumerate local boundary-return types for each left and right tail period up to symbolic period p.
Conjecture a monotone measure or pumping lemma from exhaustive runs up to 10^9 steps.
Formalize crossing sequences and the tail-phase quotient in Lean.
Derive a halting decider if the bounded-crossing lemma is proved.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean theorem that every eventually periodic input either enters a computably detected cycle or halts, with an explicit computable bound from the finite defect and periods.
approaches.failure_signature: A generated family has unbounded nonrepeating crossing sequences or simulates an unbounded counter, directly refuting the proposed bounded-crossing lemma.
approaches.missing: A viable global invariant; finite experiments cannot establish decidability.

approaches.title: Prove Smith's tape is not eventually periodic
approaches.method: Encode Wolfram machine 596440 exactly as published: state 1 on colors 0, 1, 2 writes (1, right, state 2), (2, left, state 1), (1, left, state 1); state 2 writes (2, left, state 1), (2, right, state 2), (0, right, state 1). Define eventually periodic as the existence of a center bound N and periods p, q such that the tape repeats with period p to the right of N and period q to the left. Define finite support as the case where both periodic parts are the blank symbol. Formalize Smith's doubling recurrence for the infinite initial condition, as described in his prize proof and in the public development at the Wolfram Institute Lean notes, and prove that this particular tape is not eventually periodic. Separately audit that public development against this repo's rules: no sorry, no extra axioms. The audit's job is to isolate the infinite-tape hypothesis, not to re-prove universality under a periodic background.
steps: Define machine 596440 and the two tape restrictions as Lean predicates.
Transcribe Smith's doubling construction of the infinite initial tape.
Prove that tape is not eventually periodic.
Audit the public Lean development and list every hypothesis it still assumes, in particular the non-periodic background.
Reject the module if universality is stated without that hypothesis.
approaches.decisive_result: A no-sorry lemma that Smith's infinite initial condition is not eventually periodic, plus an axiom audit showing his universality theorem uses that tape.
approaches.failure_signature: The doubling recurrence in fact produces an eventually periodic tape, or the public development's universality theorem does not depend on a non-periodic background. Either outcome would change the status of the objection rather than confirm it.
approaches.missing: The public Lean notes list open items. Closing those items under a no-sorry rule may exceed a month even though the non-periodicity lemma itself is the smaller target.

approaches.title: Decide the machine on eventually periodic tapes
approaches.method: Try to refute conventional universality by a regularity theorem. Fix an eventually periodic initial tape with left period q, right period p and a finite center of length L. The head will destroy periodicity, so the configuration space is not the finite set of phases. The attack is to find an invariant of machine 596440 that restores finiteness: a bound on the number of non-periodic cells, or a vector of local statistics (for example counts of 1s and 2s modulo a small integer) that determines the future and takes values in a finite monoid. If every space-time diagram from an eventually periodic tape is generated by a finite automaton whose state is that invariant, then halting and reachability of any finite target pattern are decidable, which refutes universality under the conventional restriction. The invariant has to be proved for all p, q and L, not checked up to a bound. A bound-only result belongs to the search approach and is not this theorem.
steps: Define the configuration graph of machine 596440 on eventually periodic tapes.
Search symbolically for a finite invariant by enumerating small moduli and local window statistics.
If a candidate invariant closes, prove it is preserved by all six transitions.
Prove that the invariant's state, plus the head state, determines the next window.
Conclude decidability of reachability, which is the anti-universality theorem.
approaches.decisive_result: A no-sorry theorem that reachability for machine 596440 on every eventually periodic tape is decidable.
approaches.failure_signature: Every candidate finite invariant fails on an explicit tape: the non-periodic region grows without a periodic residue. That kills this proof route and leaves conventional universality open.
approaches.missing: No known finite invariant for this machine. Finding one is open mathematics, not a missing dataset.

approaches.title: Search a bounded periodic-background encoding family
approaches.method: Search for a positive construction inside an explicit family, so exhaustion is a real partial result. The family is: a right-infinite periodic background of period at most 32 over the alphabet {0,1,2}, a finite program region of length at most 10^4, and a block encoding that uses only the block sizes already appearing in Smith's system-0 to system-3 schedule. For each candidate, simulate machine 596440 and test whether the successive visits of the head to the left end reproduce one full step of a fixed universal cyclic tag system (two appendants, the smallest Cook system that is already universal once cyclic-tag universality is granted) for at least 100 tag steps, with the background period unchanged outside the program. The search is exhaustive over periods and over program regions drawn from that block grammar, not over all strings of length 10^4. Publish the grammar, the seed, and the list of simulated candidates.
steps: Fix the target cyclic tag system and the block grammar before any simulation.
Enumerate background periods from 1 to 32 and program blocks within the grammar up to length 10^4.
Simulate machine 596440 from each candidate for enough steps to cover 100 tag steps or until the background is corrupted.
Accept a candidate only if the decoded tag step matches and the background period is intact.
If the grammar is exhausted with no accept, report the bound as a negative partial result.
approaches.decisive_result: Either an explicit periodic-background initial tape, of period at most 32 and program length at most 10^4, that emulates 100 steps of the chosen cyclic tag system, or a machine-readable exhaustion certificate for that grammar.
approaches.failure_signature: Exhaustion of this grammar does not refute conventional universality. The approach has failed to settle the question if the grammar is exhausted, and it has failed as a search if a candidate is accepted by one simulator and rejected by an independent reimplementation.

problems.title: Is Rule 54 computationally universal?
problems.question: Is elementary cellular automaton Rule 54 capable of universal computation, as Wolfram conjectures, or can a bound on its information transmission rule it out?
problems.known_state: Open since 2002. Martínez, Adamatzky and McIntosh catalogued Rule 54's gliders and collisions and built logic gates in 2006, but no complete emulation of a universal system exists. Wolfram's search of 100 million initial conditions (wolfram2002-ch11-21) found only repetitive and nested structures.
acceptance_criteria: A construction (glider-based or otherwise) emulating a known universal system, with the collision table verified by exhaustive simulation and formalized in Lean 4, or
A proof that Rule 54 cannot be universal (for example a regularity or transmission bound on all configurations).
falsifiers: Partial results only (new gates without a complete emulation) leave the problem open.

related_claims.label: Rule 54 shows only repetitive or nested forms in 100 million initial conditions
Class 1 and 2 cellular automata cannot be universal
Nested-pattern and additive cellular automata cannot be universal

approaches.title: Automated synthesis of a cyclic-tag emulation from the complete collision graph
approaches.method: Treat universality search as program synthesis over glider collisions. First compute the complete set of Rule 54 gliders on the standard ether up to period 120 and width 80 (de Bruijn diagrams), and the full binary collision table over all phases and gaps (outgoing gliders, phase shifts, and whether the outcome depends on the gap). Then search the collision graph for the four functional components of a Cook-style CTS emulation: stationary or slow 'tape' gliders encoding 0 and 1; a periodic left-moving 'program' stream encoding appendants; an annihilation or conversion reaction that reads the leading tape symbol; and a reaction that appends or deletes appendant material conditionally. Encode timing and spacing constraints as an SMT problem (z3, integer gaps modulo the ether period) and search for satisfying assignments that emulate a 2-appendant CTS. A solution is validated by direct simulation and then formalized as in the Rule 110 approach.
steps: Compute and publish the glider catalogue with periods, velocities and phases; compare with Martínez, Adamatzky and McIntosh 2006.
Compute the complete binary collision table and identify collisions that are gap-sensitive, the raw material for conditional behaviour.
Encode CTS-emulation components as SMT constraints over glider choices and gaps; search with increasing component sizes.
Validate any candidate by simulating a small universal CTS for 10^7 generations and decoding.
approaches.decisive_result: An explicit initial configuration (ether, finite seed, periodic stream) on which Rule 54 emulates arbitrary CTS, validated by simulation and then proved in Lean. Short of that, a proof that the collision graph restricted to gliders up to the bound lacks a conditional-append reaction, which pins down what a universal construction would need.
approaches.failure_signature: The SMT search finds no conditional reaction among gliders up to the bound; every collision outcome is independent of the data it would need to read. That is evidence that the bound is too small or that the second (impossibility) approach is the right one.
approaches.missing: Conditional (data-reading) reactions may not exist among small gliders; the search may need structures no one has catalogued.

approaches.title: Impossibility route: a potential function on glider dynamics forcing ballistic decay
approaches.method: Try to prove that Rule 54 cannot be universal in a precise sense, for example that on every finite perturbation of the ether the long-run behaviour is decidable. Strategy: (a) prove a decomposition theorem that every configuration differing from the ether on a finite set evolves, after a transient bounded in terms of the perturbation's width, into a superposition of catalogued gliders separated by ether, using a de Bruijn-diagram argument that any non-ether, non-glider region shrinks; (b) compute the full collision algebra and look for a potential Φ (a weighted glider count, or a count weighted by velocity class) that never increases in any collision and strictly decreases in some. If Φ exists and the number of gliders produced by a collision is bounded, every finite perturbation reaches, in finitely many collisions, a state of non-interacting outgoing gliders. Then 'eventual configuration' is computable, which rules out universality for the standard definition with finite seeds. The integrable reversible RCA54 of Bobenko et al., a different automaton whose name and local rule are related, has solitons that only phase-shift on collision; checking whether ECA 54's ether-restricted dynamics inherit such a conservation law is a concrete sub-question.
steps: Compute the collision algebra (outcome multiset for each glider pair, phase and gap) from the approach-1 catalogue.
Solve an integer linear program for weights making Φ non-increasing over all catalogued collisions; record strict decreases.
Attempt the decomposition theorem: prove by exhaustive de Bruijn analysis that non-glider defects shrink, giving a bound on transient length.
If both hold, formalize: decomposition plus potential implies decidability of the eventual glider content; state precisely what this excludes (universality with finite seeds on ether).
approaches.decisive_result: A proof, ideally Lean-checked, that for every finite perturbation of the ether the multiset of eventual outgoing gliders is computable. This rules out universality from finite seeds on ether, and the result states exactly which universality notions remain open (for example, infinite periodic program streams).
approaches.failure_signature: The ILP is infeasible, meaning some collision cycle increases every candidate potential (glider multiplication), or an exhaustive search finds a finite perturbation that produces unboundedly many gliders (a 'gun' or breeder). Both suggest universality is plausible and point back to approach 1.
approaches.missing: Infinite periodic program streams (as in Cook's Rule 110 proof) escape a finite-seed impossibility argument, so even success settles only one universality notion.

approaches.title: Lean-certified completeness of the Rule 54 glider catalogue up to explicit bounds
approaches.method: Both other approaches depend on knowing all gliders, and current catalogues are lists of what has been seen, not completeness theorems. Prove in Lean 4: every pattern that is spacetime-periodic on the ether, with period p ≤ P and width w ≤ W, is one of the listed gliders up to phase and translation. The method is de Bruijn-diagram enumeration. Periodic patterns of period p correspond to cycles in a finite graph whose vertices are width-2p words, so completeness reduces to enumerating cycles in finite graphs. Extract the enumeration as a certificate (cycle list plus a proof that no other cycle passes the ether boundary conditions) and check it in Lean by kernel reduction. Pick P and W so the kernel check stays feasible (P = 24 first, then extend).
steps: Define the de Bruijn graph for period-p spacetime patterns in Lean and prove the correspondence theorem (periodic pattern ⇔ graph cycle).
Generate the cycle enumeration externally for each p ≤ P with ether boundary conditions.
Check the certificate in Lean; derive the completeness theorem for the glider list.
Repeat for the binary collision table: prove that outcomes for all pairs from the complete list are as tabulated.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean theorem 'the gliders of Rule 54 on ether with period ≤ P and width ≤ W are exactly G_1 … G_k' plus a verified collision table. This does not settle universality, but turns the search space of approaches 1 and 2 from an observation into a proved object.
approaches.failure_signature: The de Bruijn graphs for useful P are too large for kernel checking (they grow as 2^(2p) vertices), capping the theorem at a P too small to include the gliders Martínez et al. used for gates.

approaches.title: Collision-circuit synthesis for Rule 54
approaches.method: Build a complete phase-resolved catalog of Rule 54 gliders and collisions, then use SAT-based spacetime synthesis to implement a universal cyclic tag system. Each gate must restore a common ether phase and tolerate every symbol context; exact traces become Lean certificates.
steps: Enumerate periodic-domain defects of width at most 60 and classify velocity and phase.
Enumerate binary and ternary collisions over all relative phases.
Synthesize fanout, delay, annihilation and conditional production modules.
Compose modules into tag steps and test at least 100,000 adversarial random steps before Lean certification.
approaches.decisive_result: A finite library of phase-restoring modules that exactly emulates a known universal cyclic tag system, plus checked traces and a compositional simulation invariant.
approaches.failure_signature: The exhaustive glider basis lacks either reliable fanout or conditional production under all contexts, closing this glider-circuit architecture within the declared bounds.
approaches.missing: Failure of one glider architecture would not prove Rule 54 nonuniversal.

approaches.title: Finite-factor obstruction to universality
approaches.method: Search for a symbolic-dynamics obstruction: a finite-state transducer or invariant cone showing every finite perturbation of each Rule 54 periodic domain decomposes into ballistic particles with ultimately periodic interactions. Infer candidate invariants from de Bruijn graphs, then prove closure and an upper bound on crossing-sequence complexity in Lean.
steps: Construct order-k de Bruijn graphs for k through 24 and minimize future-equivalence classes.
Infer conserved additive charges and particle interaction normal forms.
Attempt a finite-defect decomposition and confluence theorem.
If obtained, prove finite-defect prediction decidable and state the exact restricted nonuniversality result.
approaches.decisive_result: A machine-checked theorem that finite perturbations of specified periodic backgrounds have decidable long-term behavior via a finite particle quotient.
approaches.failure_signature: Future-equivalence class counts grow without stabilization and collision products generate unbounded novel defects, defeating the finite-factor premise.
approaches.missing: Even a finite-defect theorem may not cover arbitrary computable initial configurations.

approaches.title: Exhaustive collision census of the 2006 glider catalog
approaches.method: Take every glider and compound glider named by Martínez, Adamatzky and McIntosh 2006, on the periodic ether they use, and collide every ordered pair at every separation from 1 to 256 cells. Evolve each collision for 10^5 steps or until the configuration is a disjoint union of catalogued gliders on the ether. Two independent simulators must agree. From the resulting table, search for a finite gate set that simulates one append of a cyclic tag system: a memory-carrying glider that survives a round trip, a fan-out, and a collision sequence whose net effect is that append. New logic gates that do not compose into that append are recorded and then counted as failure, matching the problem's falsifier that partial gates leave the question open.
steps: Transcribe the 2006 glider words and ether; do not invent new names.
Collide all pairs at separations 1 through 256, cutoff 10^5 steps, with two simulators.
Classify products as ether, catalogued gliders, or a new persistent object.
Search the table for a cyclic-tag append realized as a finite collision sequence.
If found, emit the sequence as a witness; if not, emit the census and stop.
approaches.decisive_result: A collision sequence, reproduced by both simulators, whose net glider content is one step of a cyclic tag system, or a complete census up to separation 256 with no such sequence.
approaches.failure_signature: The census finds gates, oscillators or a new glider but no composition that implements a tag append. That is the partial-result failure the problem already names. Disagreement between the two simulators invalidates the census.

approaches.title: Prove a defect invariant that blocks unbounded memory
approaches.method: Attempt a negative theorem that applies to every finite perturbation of the ether, not only to the 2006 gliders. Rule 54's ether is periodic. Treat gliders as defects. Search for a conserved quantity taking values in a finite monoid: a sum of local window weights modulo m, or a pairing between left-going and right-going defects, that every space-time diagram must preserve. The universality-refuting conclusion is that the set of defects reachable from a finite perturbation is a regular language, so the diagram cannot encode an arbitrary binary work string. The conservation law has to be proved from the 8-bit table for every configuration, then specialized to finite ether perturbations. Compatibility of the invariant with a glider that stores an arbitrary string is an immediate failure of this route.
steps: Define the ether and the defect of a finite window relative to it.
Enumerate small modular weightings and test them against the 8-bit table.
Prove any surviving weighting is invariant for every configuration.
Prove that finite perturbations stay inside a regular defect language.
Conclude that no such perturbation simulates a cyclic tag system on arbitrary inputs.
approaches.decisive_result: A proof that every finite perturbation of the Rule 54 ether has space-time defect language regular, hence cannot emulate a cyclic tag system on all inputs.
approaches.failure_signature: The invariant, if it exists, still permits a defect whose internal tape is an arbitrary finite word. The route has then failed even if the invariant is true.
approaches.missing: No published conservation law of this strength. The swarm lacks a theorem, not a dataset.

approaches.title: Lean-check the published gates and their generated monoid
approaches.method: Formalize only the collisions Martínez, Adamatzky and McIntosh actually used to build gates, as kernel-checked lemmas of the same kind as the Rule 110 table, then stop at the algebra those gates generate. Represent each gate as a relation on a finite set of glider occupancy vectors. Compute the monoid generated by composition up to a stated vector length. Prove either that the monoid contains a copy of a cyclic-tag append, or that every element is a function of a finite set of counters that cannot store an arbitrary work string. This can succeed as a non-universality proof for this gate set while the wider Rule 54 question stays open, and it fails differently from the census: the census can find a new glider that this monoid never sees.
steps: Transcribe the published gate collisions and check them by kernel reduction.
Encode each gate as a relation on occupancy vectors.
Close the monoid under composition up to the stated length.
Test whether a cyclic-tag append embeds in that monoid.
If it does not, prove the monoid's memory is bounded by the counters found in the closure.
approaches.decisive_result: Either a checked embedding of one cyclic-tag step in the monoid of the 2006 gates, or a proof that this monoid cannot store an arbitrary work string.
approaches.failure_signature: The monoid is too large to close and no embedding is found. That is an inconclusive stop, not a non-universality proof. A simulator mismatch on a published gate also fails the approach.

problems.title: The Rule 30 center column
problems.question: Is the center column of Rule 30 from a single black cell non-periodic, does it have asymptotic density 1/2, and does computing its n-th cell require effort growing at least linearly in n?
problems.known_state: The three Wolfram Rule 30 Prize problems (2019), all unsolved. Non-periodicity has been verified computationally far beyond a million steps (wolfram2002-ch02-05 tests the statistical claim). Partial results exist for related sequences (surjectivity of Rule 30 on bi-infinite configurations, left-permutivity), none settles the column.
acceptance_criteria: A proof of any of the three statements, machine-checked in Lean 4.

A weaker but new result: a proven lower bound on the period (if periodic) that exceeds all computational checks, or a proof that the column is not eventually periodic under an added hypothesis made explicit.
falsifiers: Discovery of a period (would refute problem 1) or a proven density different from 1/2.

related_claims.label: Rule 30's center column shows no deviation from randomness over a million steps
Inverse problems for rule 30 are likely NP-complete
Class 3 randomness can arise without randomness in initial conditions

approaches.title: Lean: left-permutivity, Jen's two-column theorem and conditional extensions
approaches.method: Formalize the only rigorous progress on Prize problem 1 and push it as far as it goes. Rule 30 is x_i^{t+1} = x_{i−1}^t XOR (x_i^t OR x_{i+1}^t). It is left-permutive: x_{i−1}^t = x_i^{t+1} XOR (x_i^t OR x_{i+1}^t), so two adjacent columns determine everything to their left. Jen (1990, announced 1986) proved that no two columns of the single-seed pattern can both be eventually periodic. Prove in Lean: (a) the reconstruction lemma; (b) if columns i and i+1 are eventually periodic with period p, every column to the left is eventually periodic with period p; (c) Jen's theorem, from the fact that the left boundary of the light cone moves left one cell per step, contradicting periodicity of the reconstructed region. Then attempt new conditional theorems with explicit hypotheses, for example: if the center column is eventually periodic with period p from time t₀, then column +1 is not eventually periodic and its subword complexity grows at least linearly; or, the periodic-diagonal region on the left (Wolfram's observation) cannot reach the center column before time f(p).
steps: Define Rule 30 and the single-seed evolution on ℤ × ℕ; prove the light-cone and left-permutivity lemmas.
Prove the reconstruction and periodicity-propagation lemmas; derive Jen's two-column theorem.
Formulate and attempt the conditional single-column statements; record which hypotheses each needs.
Report as in the Thompson Lean reports, with axioms checked.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean module proving Jen's theorem (no two columns both eventually periodic) with only standard axioms, plus at least one new conditional theorem about the center column whose hypothesis is stated explicitly. A proof of non-periodicity itself would settle Prize problem 1.
approaches.failure_signature: All conditional extensions reduce back to assuming information about a second column; the left-permutivity method then provably cannot reach a single column without new input.
approaches.missing: Jen's theorem is tractable; a genuinely new single-column result needs a mathematical idea no one has yet found.

approaches.title: Extend the column to 10^10–10^11 bits with a pre-registered density and period test
approaches.method: Extend the known prefix beyond the published billion bits and pre-register what the extension can and cannot show. Computing n center bits needs about n²/2 cell updates, but the light cone can be trimmed: cells at distance d from the center at time t only matter if d ≤ n − t. With bit-sliced 64-wide words on GPUs this gives roughly 10^19 to 10^20 word operations for n = 10^10, which is feasible on a modest cluster. Pre-register: (a) exclusion of every eventual period p ≤ n/3 with transient ≤ n/3, using a suffix-array or Z-function scan; (b) a density test, the running deviation D(n) = #1s − n/2 compared with the law-of-iterated-logarithm envelope √(2n log log n)/2 expected for an i.i.d. fair sequence, with pass and fail bands fixed in advance; (c) block-frequency and linear-complexity profiles (Berlekamp–Massey) at block lengths 1 to 20. The result is computational evidence, recorded as data_kind 'computational', not a proof.
steps: Validate the simulator against the published billion-bit dataset (SHA-256 match).
Write result.json with hypotheses, bands and planned outputs before running beyond 10^9.
Run to n = 10^10 (stretch 10^11) with checkpointing; publish the prefix checksum and a fetch script, not the data.
Run the period-exclusion scan, the LIL density test and Berlekamp–Massey linear complexity; record verdicts.
approaches.decisive_result: A certified statement that no eventual period with transient and period each ≤ n/3 exists in the first n = 10^10 bits, and density deviations inside or outside the pre-registered LIL band. A detected period would refute problem 1 outright.
approaches.failure_signature: Compute or memory limits stop the run below 10^10, so it adds little beyond the published billion bits; or the trimming is shown to be wrong because the result disagrees with the reference prefix.
approaches.missing: GPU time on the order of 10^4 GPU-hours for 10^10 bits; less if a better light-cone trimming is found.

approaches.title: Restricted-model lower bounds: the column is not generated by small automata
approaches.method: Attack weak forms of problems 1 and 3 that are provable. Problem 3 asks for a lower bound on the effort to compute bit n, and unrestricted lower bounds are out of reach, but lower bounds against restricted models are finite questions. (a) For each base k in {2, 3, 4} and state count s ≤ 12, prove that no deterministic finite automaton with output (DFAO) reading n in base k reproduces the first N center bits. Encode as SAT (variables for transition and output tables; constraints from each prefix bit) and extract unsatisfiability certificates, which are DRAT proofs checkable by a verified checker. (b) Use Walnut to test whether the prefix is consistent with low-complexity morphic generation. (c) Prove in Lean, from (a) and the definitions, the theorem 'the center column is not k-automatic with ≤ s states'. That theorem implies, for example, that no constant-memory streaming algorithm over base-k digits of n computes the column with that much memory.
steps: Generate SAT instances for (k, s) pairs over a prefix of N = 10^6 bits (smaller if unsatisfiability is reached earlier).
Solve with a DRAT-producing solver; check proofs with a verified checker.
Formalize the DFAO definition in Lean and state the non-automaticity theorems; import the certificate check by kernel-verified decoding of the minimal refuting prefix.
Record the largest (k, s) reached and the shortest refuting prefix for each.
approaches.decisive_result: Lean-checked theorems 'the Rule 30 center column is not generated by any base-k DFAO with at most s states' for stated (k, s). These are new and weak; their value is a precise, citable lower bound in a restricted model, and any satisfiable instance that extends to 10^9 bits would be a striking structural discovery.
approaches.failure_signature: SAT instances become intractable at small s (for example s ≤ 6), giving results too weak to matter; or proofs need native_decide-level computation that Lean cannot do in kernel.

approaches.title: SAT-certified lower bounds on center-column periods
approaches.method: Encode the triangular Rule 30 light cone and the assertion that the center column is eventually p-periodic after preperiod q as SAT. Use incremental solving for all p up to a declared P and q up to Q, produce DRAT certificates for unsatisfiable cases, and verify certificates independently; formalize the reduction from a certificate to the excluded finite period claim.
steps: Generate bit-blasted Rule 30 constraints with shared subformulas.
Exclude every pair p <= 100000 and q <= 100000 using incremental SAT and symmetry reductions.
Check all UNSAT certificates with an independent verifier.
Formalize the constraint semantics and certificate implication in Lean.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean-checked theorem excluding every eventual period and preperiod in the stated rectangle, exceeding previous certified bounds.
approaches.failure_signature: A satisfying assignment reproduces from the single-cell seed and yields a genuine period; otherwise solver scaling before a novel bound defeats this approach.
approaches.missing: Finite lower bounds do not prove nonperiodicity.

approaches.title: Algebraic dependency and entropy bounds
approaches.method: Exploit left-permutivity to express center bits as Boolean polynomials of boundary variables, then seek a lemma that any eventual center period imposes repeated polynomial identities of increasing degree. Compute algebraic normal forms to identify a monotone leading monomial and formalize the resulting degree or influence lower bound.
steps: Compute exact algebraic normal forms for center bits through n = 4096.
Conjecture and prove a recurrence for a distinguished monomial or discrete derivative.
Show an eventual period would force equality of incompatible derivatives.
Formalize the recurrence and contradiction in Lean.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean theorem proving non-eventual-periodicity, or a new theorem that center-bit algebraic degree or influence grows unboundedly.
approaches.failure_signature: The proposed distinguished monomial cancels infinitely often or the derivative recurrence admits periodic center sequences, invalidating the invariant.
approaches.missing: A currently unknown invariant connecting global left-permutivity to the single seeded center column.

approaches.title: Certify a period lower bound past the published checks
approaches.method: Prove the elementary step in Lean: the Rule 30 cell is left XOR (center OR right). Then certify a long center-column prefix by blocked replay. An external bit-packed simulator emits a row hash every K steps; Lean replays each block from the certified start row and checks the hash and the center bit. The theorem is that if the center column is periodic with period p, then p exceeds N, where N is the length of the certified prefix with no period. N must be strictly larger than the longest prefix the Rule 30 prize page reports as already computed on the day the run starts. Read that horizon from the prize page first and write it into the pre-registration. A certified prefix that does not beat the published horizon is not a result under the acceptance criteria.
steps: Record the computational horizon stated on the prize page before running.
Prove the Rule 30 step function in Lean.
Emit block hashes from a bit-packed simulator for a prefix longer than that horizon.
Check every block in Lean.
Prove that absence of a repeat in the certified prefix rules out every period at most N.
approaches.decisive_result: A no-sorry theorem that any period of the center column exceeds the published computational horizon recorded at the start of the run.
approaches.failure_signature: A repeat is found, which refutes non-periodicity if it is a true period, or the certified N does not exceed the published horizon, in which case the approach has not met its own bar.
approaches.missing: Lean kernel time. If the published horizon is far beyond what blocked replay can certify in a month, this approach cannot finish as stated.

approaches.title: Prove density one half from left permutivity
approaches.method: The local rule f(l, c, r) = l XOR (c OR r) is left-permutive: for every fixed center and right, the two choices of the left neighbor give opposite outputs. Prove that permutivity, then the standard consequences that can be formalized: the global map on bi-infinite configurations is surjective, and the fair Bernoulli product measure is invariant. The prize question is not about almost every configuration. It is about the single orbit of the configuration with one black cell. The remaining lemma is equidistribution of that orbit's center cell: the visit frequency of black at the center tends to 1/2. State equidistribution as a separate theorem whose hypotheses, if any extra ergodicity assumption is used, are written explicitly. An extra assumption means the prize problem is not solved.
steps: Prove left permutivity from the XOR-OR formula.
Prove surjectivity on bi-infinite configurations.
Prove invariance of the fair Bernoulli measure.
Attempt equidistribution of the single-seed center cell with no added assumption.
If an ergodicity hypothesis is required, stop and label the prize statement unproved.
approaches.decisive_result: A no-sorry proof that the center-cell frequency along the single-seed orbit tends to 1/2, with no hypothesis beyond the rule and the initial cell.
approaches.failure_signature: The measure lemmas go through but equidistribution of this orbit needs an assumption that is itself open. The approach has then failed on the prize statement even if the lemmas are worth keeping.
approaches.missing: A proof idea that upgrades invariance of Bernoulli measure to equidistribution of one explicit orbit. That is the open step.

approaches.title: Show the center column is not 2-automatic
approaches.method: Attack the linear-effort prize by way of automatic sequences. A shortcut that computed the n-th center cell from the binary digits of n in o(n) time, uniformly, would make the sequence 2-automatic or at least would give a finite 2-kernel. Compute the 2-kernel of the center column: the subsequences u(2^k n + r) for residues r. Prove in Lean that the step function commutes with the kernel construction in the usual way for a cellular automaton. Then exhibit more distinct kernel sequences than any finite automaton of a given size can hold, using a certified prefix from the first approach as the witness for the small kernels, and a theorem that a new distinct subsequence appears at arbitrarily large scales. Refuting all linear recurrences over GF(2) up to a fixed order is a weaker lemma and should be stated separately; it does not by itself give an Ω(n) lower bound.
steps: Define the 2-kernel of the center column.
Prove the Rule 30 step constrains kernel sequences.
Certify, from a checked prefix, that the kernel already has more than M distinct sequences.
Prove distinctness persists at arbitrary scale, or isolate the missing lemma.
Separately refute linear recurrences up to an order fixed by the certified prefix, and do not call that the prize theorem.
approaches.decisive_result: A proof that the center column is not 2-automatic, together with a reduction showing that any uniform o(n) digit-based algorithm would imply automaticity. That is a form of the linear-effort lower bound, not yet a general Ω(n) time lower bound against all algorithms.
approaches.failure_signature: The kernel collapses to a finite set, or a new distinct subsequence cannot be forced past the certified prefix. Recurrence-refutation alone is a failure to reach the prize statement.
approaches.missing: A general time lower bound against arbitrary algorithms is beyond a kernel argument. This approach only targets digit-based and automatic shortcuts.

problems.title: Classify the network topologies that admit diffusion-driven instability
problems.question: For reaction networks of n species with m diffusing, which interaction sign-patterns (topologies) admit a Turing instability for some parameters, and is it true that for n >= 3 almost all topologies with at least one feedback loop do?
problems.known_state: Turing (1952) settled n = 2 (activator-inhibitor or substrate-depletion sign patterns, with the inhibitor diffusing faster). Marcon et al. (2016) and Scholes et al. (2019) enumerated 2- and 3-node topologies numerically and found many that pattern without differential diffusivity, but there is no proof characterizing the Turing-capable set for general n, and the genericity conjecture is numerical only. turing-ddi has formal status partial in the repo.
acceptance_criteria: A theorem, machine-checked in Lean 4 or at least rigorously proved, giving necessary and sufficient sign-pattern conditions for the existence of parameters producing a Turing instability for n = 3, and
An exhaustive, reproducible enumeration for n = 3 and n = 4 against which the theorem is checked.
falsifiers: A 3-node topology that the enumeration finds Turing-capable but the theorem excludes, or vice versa.
problems.data_access: None needed; verification against published topology atlases (Marcon 2016, Scholes 2019) which are open access.

related_claims.label: Turing diffusion-driven instability
Turing wavelength selection
Reaction-diffusion of morphogens accounts for biological pattern

approaches.title: Sign-pattern theorem via additive D-stability and sign stability
approaches.method: Reformulate. With linearization J at a stable steady state and diagonal diffusion D ≥ 0, a Turing instability is J stable with J − k²D unstable for some k > 0. Absorbing k² into D, the pattern P is Turing-capable (all species may diffuse) iff some realization J of P is stable but not additively D-stable, that is, J − D is unstable for some nonnegative diagonal D (Cross 1978). Lemma A: sign-stable patterns, characterized combinatorially by Quirk–Ruppert and Jeffries–Klee–van den Driessche (nonpositive diagonal, no positive 2-cycles, no cycles of length ≥ 3, nonzero determinant, a colour test), stay sign-stable when negative diagonal is added, hence are Turing-incapable. Conjecture B for n = 3: P is Turing-capable iff P is potentially stable and not sign-stable. Prove B by case analysis over which Jeffries condition fails (a 3-cycle, a positive self-loop, a mutualistic 2-cycle, or the colour test). For each case give an explicit parametric family (J(ε), D) that is stable, satisfying the 3×3 Routh–Hurwitz conditions a₁ > 0, a₃ > 0, a₁a₂ > a₃, with det(J − D) of the wrong sign or Routh–Hurwitz violated for J − D. For m < n diffusing species, D is supported on the diffusing set S, and the analogous criterion involves principal submatrices of J off S (Satnoianu et al. 2000).
steps: Prove in Lean: for 3×3 real matrices, define stability by the Routh–Hurwitz inequalities on the characteristic polynomial coefficients, and prove that the Turing condition is equivalent to 'not additively D-stable'.
Prove Lemma A (sign-stable implies Turing-incapable) from the Jeffries conditions.
For each failure mode of sign stability, construct witness families and prove the inequalities with nlinarith or polyrith.
Extend to restricted diffusion sets S ⊂ {1,2,3} and state the theorem for each m.
Check the theorem against approach 2's enumeration (any disagreement is a counterexample to B).
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean-checked theorem: for n = 3 and each diffusing set S, the Turing-capable sign patterns are exactly those satisfying an explicit combinatorial condition (conjecturally 'potentially stable and not S-restricted sign-stable'), with zero disagreements against the exhaustive enumeration.
approaches.failure_signature: The enumeration finds a potentially stable, non-sign-stable pattern that is Turing-incapable (every stable realization is additively D-stable without being sign-stable), so Conjecture B is false and the characterization needs a finer invariant.
approaches.missing: Mathlib lacks a ready Routh–Hurwitz theorem connecting coefficient inequalities to root location; for n = 3 it must be proved, or stability defined by the coefficient conditions with that equivalence proved separately.

approaches.title: Exact exhaustive enumeration for n = 3 and n = 4 with certificates
approaches.method: Decide Turing-capability for every sign pattern exactly, not by sampling. For n = 3 there are 3^9 = 19,683 patterns, about 3,400 up to relabelling. For each pattern and diffusing set S, the question ∃J consistent with P, ∃D ≥ 0 supported on S, ∃k: J stable and J − k²D unstable is a sentence in the existential theory of the reals, decidable by cylindrical algebraic decomposition or nlsat. Pipeline: (1) random-search for a numerical witness (log-uniform entries, D spanning six orders of magnitude); (2) if found, rationalize and verify exactly (rational arithmetic, Routh–Hurwitz), and emit the witness as a Lean `norm_num` lemma; (3) otherwise run Redlog CAD or z3 nlsat on the exact sentence and keep the 'unsat' result, or prove incapability from sign stability (approach 1, Lemma A). For n = 4, 3^16 ≈ 4.3 × 10^7 patterns, about 1.8 × 10^6 up to relabelling. Numerical witnesses should settle most capable patterns; the unresolved remainder goes to nlsat with a time cap, and capped cases are reported as open. Compare with the Marcon et al. 2016 and Scholes et al. 2019 atlases pattern by pattern.
steps: Canonicalize patterns under node relabelling (respecting S) and generate the work list.
Run witness search with exact rational verification; export capable witnesses as Lean lemmas.
Run CAD or nlsat on unresolved patterns; record certificates or timeouts.
Cross-check with the published atlases; publish the classification table with SHA-256 and reproduction scripts.
approaches.decisive_result: A complete n = 3 table (every pattern × S labelled capable with an exact rational witness, or incapable with a CAD/nlsat certificate or sign-stability proof), and an n = 4 table with the fraction left undecided stated. Any capable pattern that a published atlas lists as non-Turing, or the reverse, is reported.
approaches.failure_signature: CAD or nlsat times out on a substantial set of n = 3 patterns, so incapability cannot be certified and the table is incomplete even at n = 3.

approaches.title: Genericity for n ≥ 3 via counting non-sign-stable patterns and a 3-node embedding lemma
approaches.method: Prove the genericity conjecture without first characterizing every n. Embedding lemma: if a principal subpattern on 3 nodes is Turing-capable (with a stable realization), and the remaining nodes have negative self-loops, then the full pattern is Turing-capable. Proof sketch: realize the 3-node block with a witness, give other nodes strong self-damping −M, and scale off-block couplings by ε. For small ε and large M, the eigenvalues of J and of J − k²D are perturbations of the block eigenvalues plus values near −M, so stability and the instability persist by continuity of eigenvalues (Gershgorin plus a Rouché-type argument). Counting lemma: among n-node patterns with all diagonal entries negative, the fraction with no 3-node principal subpattern from the n = 3 capable list tends to 0 as n → ∞. This holds because the n = 3 list is nonempty and the C(n,3) triples are only weakly dependent, so a second-moment (Janson) bound applies. Together these give: almost all n-node patterns with negative self-loops are Turing-capable. Weaker hypotheses on the diagonal (for example, at least one self-loop) need a refined embedding.
steps: State and prove the embedding lemma (eigenvalue continuity under block-diagonal dominance) in Lean, or rigorously on paper if Mathlib's spectral continuity is insufficient.
Take the n = 3 capable list from approach 2 and prove the counting lemma via Janson's inequality.
Combine into the genericity theorem; state precisely the class of patterns (diagonal sign assumptions) it covers.
Check numerically against approach 2's n = 4 table: predicted capable fraction versus measured.
approaches.decisive_result: A theorem: the fraction of n-node sign patterns (in the stated class) that are Turing-capable tends to 1 as n → ∞, with an explicit rate, checked against the n = 4 enumeration.
approaches.failure_signature: The embedding lemma fails because coupling to the other nodes destroys stability or instability in ways small ε cannot control for some sign configurations, or the n = 4 enumeration shows a capable fraction inconsistent with the bound.
approaches.missing: Eigenvalue-perturbation results in Mathlib are thin; the Lean version may need to be replaced by a rigorous paper proof.

approaches.title: Quantifier-eliminate all three-node sign patterns
approaches.method: Represent a three-species Jacobian with prescribed zero/sign entries and diagonal diffusion with one to three positive diffusivities. Turing capability is an existential semialgebraic formula: stability at wave number zero plus instability for some q > 0. Use cylindrical algebraic decomposition per sign pattern, then translate compact certificates into determinant, trace and Routh-Hurwitz lemmas checked in Lean.
steps: Canonicalize all 3-node signed directed graphs under permutation and global rescaling.
Write exact Routh-Hurwitz and diffusion-shift inequalities.
Run exact quantifier elimination and extract parameter witnesses or infeasibility certificates.
Prove the classification theorem and check every graph against numerical witnesses.
approaches.decisive_result: Necessary and sufficient conditions for every canonical 3-node sign pattern, with exact rational witnesses for capable classes and checked algebraic contradictions for incapable classes.
approaches.failure_signature: Quantifier elimination cannot finish after decomposition, or numerical capability disagrees with an exact certificate, exposing an encoding error.
approaches.missing: Efficient proof-certificate translation from quantifier elimination into Lean.

approaches.title: Asymptotic capability fraction for random sign graphs
approaches.method: Define an explicit random topology ensemble with independent directed edges, signs and m diffusers. For n = 3 through 8, estimate existence of Turing parameters by global optimization followed by interval verification, stratified by feedback-cycle signatures. Fit finite-size scaling and seek constructive sufficient conditions based on an embedded capable motif plus weak couplings.
steps: Pre-register graph ensemble, parameter box and interval verification criterion.
Enumerate n <= 5 exactly and sample at least 100000 graphs for each larger n and m.
Verify candidate instabilities with interval eigenvalue bounds.
Prove an embedding lemma that preserves instability under sufficiently small added couplings.
approaches.decisive_result: A verified lower bound on the capable fraction with 99% binomial intervals and a theorem showing a stated motif family remains capable for all n.
approaches.failure_signature: Capability fraction remains bounded away from one after conditioning on feedback, or supposed motif extensions lose instability under every admissible coupling.
approaches.missing: Sampling cannot by itself settle the almost-all conjecture.

approaches.title: Formalize equal-diffusion impossibility and the n=2 list
approaches.method: Two theorems, both classical, both absent as checked lemmas. First, for every dimension n, if the diffusion matrix is a scalar multiple of the identity, every eigenvalue of J minus q squared D is an eigenvalue of J shifted by a non-positive real, so Hurwitz stability of J implies stability at every wave number. Equal diffusion cannot create a Turing instability. This does not contradict Marcon et al., who found patterning by mechanisms other than that linear instability; the theorem's statement must say diffusion-driven linear instability, not patterning. Second, for n = 2, derive the necessary and sufficient sign patterns: the inhibitor diffuses faster, and the Jacobian signs are the activator-inhibitor pattern or the substrate-depletion pattern. Use the Routh–Hurwitz criteria on the quadratic characteristic polynomial. Hypotheses are the signs and which species diffuse.
steps: Define the Jacobian, the diagonal diffusion matrix and the dispersion relation.
Prove the equal-diffusion theorem for general n.
Specialize to n = 2 and compute the Hurwitz inequalities.
Case-split the sign patterns and prove the two classical patterns are exactly the Turing-capable ones.
Audit axioms.
approaches.decisive_result: No-sorry theorems: equal diffusivities forbid a Turing instability in every dimension, and for two species the Turing-capable sign patterns are exactly the two classical ones.
approaches.failure_signature: A concrete 2-by-2 sign pattern outside those two classes, with numerical rates, that is stable without diffusion and unstable at some wave number. That would falsify the classification.

approaches.title: Exact n=3 sign-pattern census by interval bounds
approaches.method: Enumerate all 3^9 = 19683 sign patterns in {-1, 0, +1}^{3×3}. Quotient by simultaneous permutation of the three species only after the raw census, so the quotient cannot hide a disagreement. A pattern is Turing-capable if there exist positive rate magnitudes and a non-negative diffusion vector, not a scalar multiple of the identity, such that J is Hurwitz and J minus q squared D is not Hurwitz for some q > 0. Hurwitz for 3×3 is the three Routh–Hurwitz inequalities on the characteristic polynomial. Search by log-uniform samples of the nonzero magnitudes in [10^{-2}, 10^{2}], 200 draws per pattern, and a log grid of q. Every pattern not decided by a sample goes to interval branch-and-bound on the log-magnitudes. Capable means a concrete witness box.
