Incapable means the parameter domain is covered by boxes that violate the conditions. A pattern still unresolved below a minimum box width is a failure of the census, not a silent negative. Compare witnesses with the Turing-instability labels in Marcon et al. 2016 and Scholes et al. 2019, not with their broader patterning labels.
steps: Enumerate the 19683 sign patterns and the diffusion supports.
Apply the Routh–Hurwitz test to samples and to the q grid.
Branch-and-bound every undecided pattern with interval arithmetic.
Emit a witness or a covering certificate for each pattern.
Match the capable set against the Turing labels in the two atlases and list every disagreement.
approaches.decisive_result: A complete partition of the 19683 patterns into capable and incapable, with a witness or a covering certificate for each, and an empty disagreement list against the published Turing labels or an explicit list of disagreements.
approaches.failure_signature: More than 1 percent of patterns remain unresolved, or a published Turing-capable network is certified incapable, or the converse. Either is a failed census or a failed atlas entry, and the approach must say which.

approaches.title: Monte Carlo the n=4 genericity conjecture
approaches.method: The genericity claim is that for n at least 3, almost all topologies with a feedback loop are Turing-capable. For n = 4 an exact census of 3^16 patterns is not the target. Draw 2000 sign patterns uniformly among those whose interaction digraph contains at least one directed cycle, assign diffusion to a non-empty random subset of species, and test 100 log-uniform rate draws with the same Routh–Hurwitz and wave-number sweep as the n = 3 census. Estimate the capable fraction and a Clopper–Pearson 95 percent interval. Almost-all is pre-registered as a fraction above 0.9. A cycle is required in the sample by construction, so the estimate is conditional on that event. This sample can refute the conjecture and cannot prove it.
steps: Sample 2000 four-species sign patterns conditioned on having a directed cycle.
Sample diffusion supports that are not scalar.
Test 100 rate draws per pattern with the Hurwitz criteria.
Compute the capable fraction and the Clopper–Pearson interval.
Declare the conjecture refuted for n = 4 if the interval lies below 0.9, and unrefuted otherwise.
approaches.decisive_result: A Clopper–Pearson 95 percent interval for the Turing-capable fraction among 4-node cyclic sign patterns. The conjecture is refuted for this n if the interval lies entirely below 0.9.
approaches.failure_signature: The interval covers both sides of 0.9, so the sample does not decide the conjecture. That is a failed test, not evidence for the conjecture. Patterns found capable only because diffusion was accidentally scalar are a bug, not a result.

problems.title: The exact scope of Hamilton's rule
problems.question: Under precisely which population-genetic models is Hamilton's rule rb > c (i) a theorem with predictive content, (ii) an identity with no content beyond the Price equation, and (iii) false?
problems.known_state: Nowak, Tarnita and Wilson (2010) argued the rule is almost never a theorem and when general is tautological; Gardner, West and Wild (2011) replied that the regression form is exact and general. Birch and Okasha (2015) separate the readings. The dispute is partly about theorem statements, which makes it formalizable; no formalization exists. The repo records hamilton-rule as proved in the regression form and hamilton-haplodiploidy as refuted.
acceptance_criteria: A Lean 4 development stating the general regression form, the additive-fitness form and a frequency-dependent counterexample as separate theorems, each proved or refuted, with the model assumptions as explicit hypotheses.
A short statement of which disputed claims in the 2010-2011 exchange correspond to which formal theorem.
falsifiers: A formal model in which the regression form fails to predict the direction of allele-frequency change would refute Gardner et al.'s generality claim.
problems.data_access: None needed for the formal part; empirical follow-up can use pedigreed cooperative-breeder datasets.

related_claims.label: Hamilton's rule
Haplodiploidy hypothesis for eusociality
Local mate competition sex ratio

approaches.title: Lean: Price equation and the regression Hamilton's rule as an exact finite identity
approaches.method: Formalize the finite-population statements both sides of the 2010–2011 dispute rely on. Population: a Finset of individuals with breeding value g_i, social partners' breeding value g'_i and fitness w_i (real, mean w̄ > 0). Theorem 1 (Price, no transmission bias): w̄ Δḡ = Cov(w, g). Theorem 2 (least-squares decomposition): with c := −β_{wg·g'} and b := β_{wg'·g} the partial regression coefficients from the 2×2 normal equations (assuming the regressors' covariance matrix is nonsingular), Cov(w, g) = Var(g)(r b − c) with r := Cov(g', g)/Var(g). Corollary (regression HR): if Var(g) > 0, then Δḡ > 0 ⇔ r b > c. Theorem 3 (content condition): if fitness is exactly additive, w_i = α − c₀ g_i + b₀ g'_i, then the regression b, c equal b₀, c₀ in every population state, so the rule predicts change from parameters fixed in advance. Theorem 4: if fitness has an interaction term d g_i g'_i, the regression b and c depend on the population state, so b and c measured in one generation do not predict the next. These separate reading (ii), an identity, from reading (i), a theorem with content.
steps: Define finite-population mean, covariance and partial regression coefficients over Finset sums in Lean.
Prove Theorems 1 and 2 and the corollary with field_simp, ring and positivity.
Prove Theorem 3 (parameter recovery under additivity) and Theorem 4 (state dependence under synergy), giving explicit rational states for the latter.
Write the mapping document: each disputed sentence from Nowak et al. 2010, Gardner et al. 2011 and Birch and Okasha 2015 assigned to Theorems 1–4 or to approach 2's counterexamples.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean module with Theorems 1–4 compiled with only standard axioms, and a mapping table assigning each disputed claim to a formal statement. This settles which claims are identities and which have content under which hypotheses.
approaches.failure_signature: None expected for Theorems 1–3, which are classical. The approach fails as a resolution if the mapping shows the disputants mean incompatible definitions of 'Hamilton's rule' that no single formal statement captures; the mapping would then document the equivocation instead.

approaches.title: Formal counterexamples: synergistic games where parameter-based rb > c mispredicts
approaches.method: Settle reading (iii), when the rule is false, by explicit, Lean-checked counterexamples in standard population-genetic models. Model: a two-player game with payoffs to a focal individual: cooperate against cooperate R = b − c + d, cooperate against defect −c, defect against cooperate b, defect against defect 0. Here d is the synergy term, and assortment is given by relatedness r through the probability that partners share type. Under weak selection, with linear fitness and the probability of a cooperator partner given focal type p_C = r + (1 − r)p, the expected change in cooperator frequency has sign (r b − c) + d·φ(r, p), with φ an explicit polynomial. Choose rational (b, c, d, r, p) with r b > c but Δp < 0, and the reverse, and prove both in Lean by norm_num. Also prove the general form, the generalized Hamilton's rule with the synergy correction (Queller's form), as a theorem, so the counterexample marks where the simple rule's scope ends. Second family: a frequency-dependent threshold game where the sign of Δp flips with p at fixed (b, c, r), showing that no fixed parameter pair predicts the direction everywhere.
steps: Define the game, assortment and expected allele-frequency change in Lean.
Derive the closed form for Δp and prove the synergy-corrected rule.
Prove two explicit counterexample instances and the frequency-flip instance with norm_num.
Add these as the (iii) entries of the approach-1 mapping table.
approaches.decisive_result: Lean theorems exhibiting model states in which the parameter-based rule r b > c and the actual direction of selection disagree, alongside a theorem stating the corrected rule. This is the formal refutation the problem's falsifier asks about for the parameter reading, while approach 1 shows the regression reading is never refuted.
approaches.failure_signature: None for the mathematics. The approach fails as a contribution if reviewers judge the model class non-standard; mitigate by using the exact models of van Veelen et al. 2017 and Lehmann and Keller 2006.

approaches.title: Computational phase map of when parameter-based Hamilton's rule predicts selection
approaches.method: Map the boundary between readings (i) and (iii) across model space, not just at isolated counterexamples. Model classes: Wright–Fisher island model (n demes ∈ {2, 5, 20}, migration m ∈ [0.001, 0.5]); Moran process on cycles, regular graphs (degree 3–10) and random graphs with N ∈ {20, 50, 200}; two-player games with synergy d ∈ [−b, b]; and multiplicative versus additive fitness, at selection strengths δ from 10^-4 to 1. In each cell compute exactly (small N, linear algebra on the Markov chain) or by simulation with 10^6 replicates (larger N) the fixation probability of a single cooperator relative to neutral 1/N. Compare three predictors: parameter HR with model b, c and pedigree or identity-by-descent r; the weak-selection inclusive-fitness condition (Taylor–Frank); and regression HR, which holds by approach 1. Output the fraction of model space where parameter HR gives the right sign, as a function of δ and d.
steps: Implement exact Markov-chain fixation for small graphs and validated Monte Carlo for larger ones.
Pre-register the predictors and the agreement metric (sign agreement and, where nonzero, rank correlation of effect sizes).
Sweep the grid; publish the phase maps with code and seeds.
Identify the analytic boundary (for example agreement whenever d = 0 and δ → 0) and feed it back to approach 1 as a theorem to prove.
approaches.decisive_result: Phase maps showing, for each model class, the region where parameter-based r b > c correctly predicts the direction of selection. The pre-stated expectation is 100% agreement at d = 0, δ → 0, with measured degradation as |d| and δ grow; a region of disagreement at d = 0 under weak selection would itself be notable.
approaches.failure_signature: Monte Carlo noise at small fixation-probability differences makes signs undecidable in large parts of the grid (Wilson intervals overlapping 1/N), so the map is mostly 'unresolved'.

approaches.title: Lean taxonomy of Hamilton-rule statements
approaches.method: Formalize finite populations as weighted probability spaces and allele-frequency change as a covariance identity. Separate three statements: the Price-equation regression identity, an additive causal fitness theorem with exogenous coefficients, and a frequency-dependent predictive rule. Prove the first two under explicit hypotheses and encode a minimal counterexample to the third.
steps: Define reproductive value, fitness, genotype and social-partner genotype on a finite probability space.
Prove the Price covariance identity and least-squares decomposition including zero-variance cases.
Derive rb > c iff positive allele-frequency change under additive linear fitness and transmission assumptions.
Exhaustively search two- and three-player games for a rational frequency-dependent counterexample and check it in Lean.
approaches.decisive_result: A no-sorry Lean module whose theorem boundaries exactly identify when rb > c is an identity, a predictive theorem, or false, including a checked finite countermodel.
approaches.failure_signature: The proposed countermodel disappears when relatedness and costs are defined consistently, or the predictive theorem needs assumptions equivalent to its conclusion.

approaches.title: Exhaustive finite-population boundary map
approaches.method: Enumerate finite haploid models with population size 2 through 8, binary action, mutation, assortment and all rational payoff tables on a coarse grid. Compute exact one-generation allele change, regression r, b and c, and causal intervention effects. Classify disagreements among identity, additive and causal readings and mine minimal assumption sets with decision trees.
steps: Predefine each Hamilton-rule estimator and degeneracy handling.
Enumerate transition kernels using exact rational arithmetic.
Record minimal models where each reading predicts the wrong sign.
Generalize recurring boundaries into conjectured lemmas for Lean.
approaches.decisive_result: A complete exact atlas for the declared model class, with minimal counterexamples and zero unexplained disagreements between implementation and formal definitions.
approaches.failure_signature: Classification depends primarily on arbitrary regression conventions rather than model structure, preventing a stable scope taxonomy.

approaches.title: Three Lean theorems for the three readings of rb > c
approaches.method: Formalize the Birch–Okasha separation as three theorems with disjoint hypotheses. Price's identity first: the change in mean breeding value equals the covariance of fitness and breeding value divided by mean fitness, plus the expected fitness-weighted transmission term. Under fair meiosis the transmission term is zero, so the sign of allele-frequency change is the sign of that covariance. Regression form: define r as the least-squares regression of partner genotype on actor genotype, and b, c as the partial regressions of fitness on partner and actor genotype. Prove that r b - c equals the covariance ratio by the normal equations, so the regression form predicts the sign of frequency change whenever the transmission term vanishes. This is an identity, and the theorem should say so. Additive form: fitness is exactly 1 - c x + b y with b, c constant and y the partner phenotype. Prove the same sign prediction with genealogical relatedness in place of the regression. Counterexample theorem: with fitness 1 - c x + b x y, b and c frozen at one frequency do not preserve the sign at another frequency. State the 2010–2011 correspondence in the module docstring: Nowak, Tarnita and Wilson attack dynamic sufficiency of inclusive-fitness maximization; Gardner, West and Wild defend the regression identity; those are different theorems.
steps: Prove Price's identity and the fair-meiosis corollary.
Prove the regression form from the normal equations, labeled as an identity.
Prove the additive constant-b, constant-c form with genealogical relatedness.
Prove a frequency-dependent counterexample to the frozen additive predictor.
Map each theorem onto the 2010 and 2011 claims in the module documentation.
approaches.decisive_result: Three no-sorry theorems with explicit hypotheses, plus a short map from those theorems onto the 2010–2011 dispute.
approaches.failure_signature: A model inside the regression theorem's hypotheses where the regression form has the wrong sign of allele-frequency change. That would refute the identity and the formalization together.

approaches.title: Exact Moran chain where frozen rb > c has the wrong sign
approaches.method: Give a finite witness that does not rely on Monte Carlo error. Population of N = 6 haploid individuals, reproduction a Moran birth-death update, interaction in three fixed pairs so genealogical relatedness inside a pair is 1 and between pairs is 0. Phenotype x in {0,1}. Fitness w = 1 - c x + b x y with b = 5 and c = 1, where y is the partner phenotype. The state is the integer count of cooperators, 0 through 6, and the chain is written in closed form. The additive predictor freezes b and c at frequency 1/2 by an ordinary least-squares regression on the exact stationary-conditional fitnesses at states with three cooperators, then is applied at every other state. The regression predictor is refit at each state. Compare signs with the exact expected frequency change. Pre-register success as: the refit regression matches the sign of expected change at every non-absorbing state where the absolute expected change exceeds 0, and the frozen predictor disagrees at least at one endpoint state.
steps: Write the 7-state Moran transition matrix for the paired population and the synergistic payoff.
Compute exact expected frequency change at each state.
Fit the frozen additive regression at the three-cooperator states.
Refit the regression at every state.
Compare signs and emit the disagreement table.
approaches.decisive_result: An exact table, with rational arithmetic, where the refit regression matches every nonzero expected frequency change and the additive coefficients frozen at frequency 1/2 disagree in sign at least once.
approaches.failure_signature: The frozen additive predictor agrees in sign at every state, or the refit regression disagrees. The second outcome would contradict the regression identity and fail the formalization too.

approaches.title: Separate the regression identity from ESS maximization
approaches.method: Nowak, Tarnita and Wilson's target is dynamic sufficiency of inclusive-fitness maximization, not the regression identity. Use the same Moran chain as the sign witness. Compute its exact stationary distribution by solving the linear balance equations on the transient states with mutation probability u = 0.01 each birth, so the chain is irreducible. Define the inclusive-fitness ESS as the strategy that maximizes r b_marg - c with genealogical r from the pair structure and b_marg the marginal benefit at that frequency. Pre-register the comparison: the stationary mean frequency is not within 0.05 of the ESS frequency, while the one-step regression identity still holds at every state. That package shows an identity with predictive content for one-step change and no content for the long-run optimum. It fails differently from the sign witness, which never looks at the stationary distribution.
steps: Add mutation u = 0.01 and solve the stationary distribution exactly.
Compute the inclusive-fitness ESS frequency from the marginal benefit.
Check the one-step regression identity at each state.
Compare stationary mean frequency to the ESS with tolerance 0.05.
Report the pair of outcomes as the scope statement for this model.
approaches.decisive_result: Exact stationary mean at least 0.05 away from the inclusive-fitness ESS, together with the regression identity holding at every state of the same chain.
approaches.failure_signature: The stationary mean sits within 0.05 of the ESS. This model then does not witness the gap Nowak et al. claim, and another payoff would be a new approach rather than a rescue of this one.

problems.title: Rigorous classification of attractors in dynamical phyllotaxis
problems.question: In the Douady-Couder class of models (new primordium placed at the point of least repulsion from existing ones on a growing cylinder or disc), what is the complete set of attractors and their basins as the growth parameter varies, and does the golden-angle Fibonacci branch have full-measure basin for small growth parameter?
problems.known_state: Douady and Couder (1992) showed numerically and experimentally that the Fibonacci branch is selected; Levitov (1991) explained the energetics; Atela, Golé and Hotton (2002) proved convergence to Fibonacci lattices for a cylindrical model under restrictions. Pennybacker, Shipman and Newell (2015) review the gap: no rigorous classification covering Lucas and bijugate branches, basin boundaries, or the disc geometry. Thompson's phyllotaxis claims (ch14) sit on this.
acceptance_criteria: A theorem characterizing the attractors for the cylindrical Douady-Couder map over a stated parameter range, including the Lucas branch, with proof (Lean 4 or rigorous computer-assisted interval proof).
Numerical basin maps matching the theorem.
falsifiers: Numerical discovery of an attractor outside the classified set.
problems.data_access: None needed; sunflower and cone parastichy counts in the repo (thompson1917-ch14-05/06 tests) can check predictions.

related_claims.label: Spirals of sunflower, thistle and cone are deformations of helices on a stem
Parastichy numbers change when the structure varies greatly in size
Right- and left-handed parastichy directions occur about equally often
Which parastichies are conspicuous depends on leaf proportions, not on divergence
Sunflower spirals intersect isogonally, rarely orthogonally

approaches.title: Computer-assisted proof of attractors via interval Newton and Conley–Morse graphs
approaches.method: Use the Atela–Golé–Hotton reduction: in the cylindrical hard-disk version of the Douady–Couder model (each new primordium at the lowest available position at distance ≥ D from existing ones on a cylinder of circumference 1), the dynamics reduce to a finite-dimensional map on 'fronts', the chains of most recent primordia. Rhombic lattices (Fibonacci, Lucas, bijugate and other parastichy pairs) are fixed points of this map up to translation. For the smooth-repulsion version (energy Σ exp(−|x − x_j|/λ) or a power law), the step map is piecewise smooth. Plan: (a) for each candidate branch (m, n), enclose the fixed point over parameter boxes in D (or Γ) with the interval Newton or Krawczyk operator in Arb/FLINT or CAPD, and enclose the Jacobian spectrum inside the unit disk to certify local attraction; (b) for global classification, build a Conley–Morse graph over a box grid of the reduced state space for each parameter box (the Arai et al. 2009 database method), certifying that every recurrent set is one of the enclosed fixed points; (c) the Lucas and bijugate branches enter as additional Morse sets with their own parameter ranges.
steps: Implement the front map exactly (hard-disk model) and the smooth-repulsion map; reproduce Douady–Couder bifurcation diagrams numerically.
Certify fixed points and stability with interval Newton or Krawczyk across D ∈ [D_min, 0.5] in boxes, adaptively refined.
Compute Conley–Morse graphs per parameter box; check that the Morse sets match the certified fixed points.
Publish the certified bifurcation diagram and code; describe precisely the parameter range covered.
approaches.decisive_result: A computer-assisted theorem: for all D in a stated range, the only attractors of the cylindrical front map are the certified lattice fixed points, which include the Fibonacci and Lucas branches with explicit ranges, and every other initial front converges to one of them. Basin boundaries are bounded by the Morse decomposition.
approaches.failure_signature: Conley–Morse graphs at feasible resolutions contain Morse sets that are not single fixed points (unresolved recurrent sets) in significant parameter ranges, or the discontinuities of the hard-disk map break the interval Newton enclosures near bifurcations.
approaches.missing: The disc geometry (non-cylindrical, radially varying spacing) is out of scope for this reduction; the result would cover only the cylinder.

approaches.title: Lean: lattice parastichy theorems from continued fractions
approaches.method: Formalize the static half of the theory, which every dynamical claim refers to and which is classical. For the lattice of points (kα mod 1, k·h), k ∈ ℤ, on a cylinder, with divergence α and rise h, prove: (a) the visible opposed parastichy pairs, the two shortest lattice vectors forming a basis and pointing in opposite directions, have numbers (q_j, q_{j+1}) given by consecutive denominators of convergents or intermediate fractions of α; (b) as h decreases, the visible pair changes exactly at the h-values where three vectors have equal length (triangular lattice points), and the sequence of pairs is the convergent sequence; (c) for α = the golden angle fraction (3 − √5)/2, all visible pairs are consecutive Fibonacci numbers, for α = 1/(3 + 1/φ) (the Lucas angle) consecutive Lucas numbers, and bijugate lattices give 2× Fibonacci pairs. Mathlib has generalized continued fractions (GenContFract) and Fibonacci (Nat.fib), so most groundwork exists.
steps: Define the cylindrical lattice, visible parastichy pairs and the shortest-vector basis in Lean.
Prove the convergent characterization using Mathlib's continued-fraction API and best-approximation lemmas.
Specialize to golden, Lucas and bijugate cases; prove the Fibonacci and Lucas statements.
Write a report linking each theorem to Thompson's ch14 claims in the repo.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean module proving that the visible opposed parastichy numbers of the golden-angle lattice are consecutive Fibonacci numbers for every rise h, with the Lucas and bijugate analogues. It does not classify dynamical attractors, but certifies the lattice side that approach 1's fixed points are identified by.
approaches.failure_signature: Mathlib's best-approximation lemmas for continued fractions are not in the form needed, and proving them from scratch exceeds the time budget.

approaches.title: Simulated basin measures tested against citizen-science sunflower counts
approaches.method: Turn the model into a quantitative prediction about real plants. Simulate the Douady–Couder disc model and the cylindrical model over a slowly decreasing growth parameter Γ (the ontogenetic path from seedling to capitulum), starting from initial fronts sampled from a stated distribution (cotyledon arrangement: decussate or two-fold at stated rates, plus Gaussian positional noise σ ∈ {0.01, 0.03, 0.1}). Record the terminal parastichy pair class (Fibonacci, Lucas, double Fibonacci, other) and the basin measures with Wilson intervals from 10^5 runs per setting. Pre-register predicted class frequencies at each σ and compare with the Swinton et al. 2016 sunflower data and the repo's thompson1917-ch14-05/06 parastichy count tests, using a multinomial likelihood-ratio test. The pre-registered rule: the model supports the data if some σ in the grid gives p > 0.05 for the class distribution; it is refuted if all σ give p < 0.001 or if the model cannot produce the observed non-Fibonacci classes at all.
steps: Implement disc and cylinder simulators with an inhibition-field placement rule; validate against Douady and Couder 1996 diagrams.
Write result.json with predictions per σ and the decision rule before downloading the Swinton data.
Run 10^5 simulations per setting; estimate class frequencies.
Fetch the sunflower data, classify heads by published parastichy counts, run the multinomial test.
approaches.decisive_result: A pre-registered verdict on whether the Douady–Couder model, with one noise parameter, reproduces the observed frequencies of Fibonacci, Lucas and other classes in sunflowers. If it does, the basin measures are what the rigorous classification must explain.
approaches.failure_signature: Model frequencies cannot match the observed share of non-Fibonacci heads for any σ, or the data lack enough class detail to distinguish Lucas from other non-Fibonacci heads (then inconclusive, underpowered).

approaches.title: Interval-certified cylinder attractors
approaches.method: Fix a smooth finite-range repulsion kernel and reduce the cylindrical placement process to a finite-memory map after proving an exponential tail bound. Use interval Newton and cone conditions to certify fixed or periodic lattice branches, then cover the state space with boxes whose images enter certified basins or declared unresolved sets.
steps: Specify kernel, growth parameter interval and finite-memory truncation error.
Continue Fibonacci, Lucas and bijugate branches with interval arithmetic.
Certify hyperbolicity and trapping neighborhoods.
Run a validated box-cover basin computation and formally check interval certificates.
approaches.decisive_result: For a nontrivial growth interval, a rigorous list of all attractors and basin-volume bounds whose uncovered state-space measure is below 10^-6.
approaches.failure_signature: Persistent positive-measure unresolved boxes or a certified additional attractor outside the proposed branches disproves completeness.
approaches.missing: Validated numerics infrastructure for the model's discontinuous least-repulsion placement rule.

approaches.title: Empirical basin frequencies from randomized primordia
approaches.method: Pre-register a computational experiment over growth parameters and perturbation amplitudes. Sample 100000 initial states per stratum using a declared uniform phase measure, simulate until convergence diagnostics stabilize, classify parastichy pairs, and estimate basin probabilities with simultaneous multinomial confidence intervals. Compare cylinder and disc geometries.
steps: Fix repulsion kernel, numerical precision, initial-state measure and attractor classifier.
Validate convergence classifications against high-precision reruns.
Estimate basin probabilities on an adaptive parameter grid.
Search rare trajectories for unknown attractors and hand them to interval certification.
approaches.decisive_result: A reproducible basin atlas with 99% lower confidence bound above 0.999 for the Fibonacci basin in any claimed small-growth interval, or a measured non-Fibonacci mass exceeding 0.001.
approaches.failure_signature: Classifier instability under precision doubling or discovery of persistent unclassified trajectories above 0.1% prevents the full-measure inference.
approaches.missing: Simulation cannot prove full measure.

approaches.title: Interval-certify cylindrical Fibonacci and Lucas branches
approaches.method: Implement the discrete cylindrical map exactly as defined by Atela, Golé and Hotton 2003, whose fixed points are cylindrical lattices and whose bifurcation parameter is the growth parameter of their diagram. Do not substitute a different potential. On a uniform grid of that parameter across the interval their paper analyzes, certify attracting cycles by interval Newton on the return map: a cycle is certified when an interval box maps into itself and the interval derivative excludes magnitude 1 or greater. Classify certified limits by parastichy pair: consecutive Fibonacci numbers, consecutive Lucas numbers, or the bijugate doubles. A trajectory whose interval enclosure stays away from every classified cycle is an unclassified attractor. The golden-angle branch is the divergence 2π/φ^2 with φ = (1 + sqrt(5))/2. Full Lebesgue measure of its basin is not claimed by a grid; the grid certifies which cycles exist.
steps: Encode the Atela–Golé–Hotton cylindrical map from the paper, not a proxy.
Sweep their growth parameter on a stated grid.
Certify attracting cycles by interval Newton.
Label each cycle as Fibonacci, Lucas, bijugate, or unclassified.
Emit the certified partition of the parameter interval.
approaches.decisive_result: A certified partition of the paper's parameter interval into basins of Fibonacci, Lucas and bijugate cycles, with every grid point accounted for.
approaches.failure_signature: An interval-certified attractor that is none of those families. That is the falsifier the problem states: an attractor outside the classified set.

approaches.title: Formalize the Atela–Golé–Hotton fixed-point theorem
approaches.method: Turn the 2003 existence-and-stability argument into Lean lemmas, restricted to the hypotheses printed in that paper. The first theorem is the characterization of fixed points as cylindrical lattices whose divergence angle is a noble number, with the Fibonacci and Lucas branches identified by their continued-fraction endings. The second is stability of those fixed points on the branches where the paper proves stability, with the same restrictions. Do not extend the theorem to the disc, to bijugate branches the paper does not cover, or to a full-measure basin. Those are different claims. A proof that uses an unformalized estimate must keep that estimate as a named hypothesis. The module is a success only if the named hypotheses are exactly the paper's.
steps: Define the cylindrical lattice and the divergence angle.
Prove the fixed-point characterization and the continued-fraction labeling.
Formalize the stability estimates under the paper's restrictions.
Leave any unformalized estimate as a named hypothesis and list it.
Audit axioms.
approaches.decisive_result: A no-sorry fixed-point theorem and a stability theorem whose hypotheses match Atela, Golé and Hotton 2003, including the Lucas branch where their proof includes it.
approaches.failure_signature: A numerically certified attractor from the interval sweep lies outside the theorem's fixed-point list inside the theorem's parameter range. The formalization and the sweep then disagree.
approaches.missing: The paper is a long real-analysis argument. A month is enough to formalize definitions and perhaps the fixed-point labeling, and unlikely to finish every stability estimate.

approaches.title: Monte Carlo basin volumes on the disc
approaches.method: The disc geometry is the gap the cylindrical theorem does not close. Implement the Douady–Couder disc rule: each new primordium is placed at the angular minimum of the repulsive field of the existing primordia on a growing disc, with the growth parameter in the same role as in their 1992 simulations. Sweep 200 parameter values. At each, launch 500 random initial angles and place 300 primordia. Classify the last 50 divergence angles by distance to the golden angle, the Lucas angle, and the bijugate angles. Estimate basin volume as the fraction of seeds in each class, with a bootstrap percentile interval of 1000 resamples. An unclassified attractor has angular error above 10^{-3} radians from every listed noble angle over those 50 primordia and estimated measure above 0.01. This atlas can falsify a proposed complete list and cannot prove full measure.
steps: Implement the disc placement rule from Douady and Couder 1992.
Sweep 200 growth parameters and 500 seeds, 300 primordia each.
Classify terminal divergence angles against the noble list.
Bootstrap the basin-volume estimates.
Flag any class with measure above 0.01 that is not on the list.
approaches.decisive_result: A basin-volume table with bootstrap intervals. The classified list fails if any unclassified class has estimated measure above 0.01.
approaches.failure_signature: Discovery of such an unclassified attractor. Failure of a different kind is a simulator bug: two implementations disagree on the terminal angle of a shared seed by more than 10^{-3} radians.

problems.title: Lewontin's paradox of variation
problems.question: Why does nucleotide diversity scale so weakly with census population size across species, and can linked selection plus demographic history account quantitatively for the gap predicted by neutral theory?
problems.known_state: Kimura's neutral theory predicts heterozygosity proportional to 4Nu; observed diversity spans about three orders of magnitude while census sizes span more than twelve (Lewontin 1974). Leffler et al. (2012) compiled diversity across 167 species; Corbett-Detig et al. (2015) argued linked selection explains part of it; Buffalo (2021) estimated the diversity-census slope with phylogenetic correction and found linked selection insufficient. The quantitative residual is unexplained.
acceptance_criteria: A pre-registered test combining a current polymorphism compilation with census-size and range-size estimates (GBIF occurrence extents from the organisms layer) and recombination-rate or genome-size covariates, with explicit quantitative predictions from each hypothesis (neutral, linked selection, boom-bust demography) stated before analysis.
A verdict on whether linked selection models fitted to measured recombination landscapes close the gap.
falsifiers: If linked-selection models with measured parameters predict the observed slope, the paradox is resolved; if the residual stays at orders of magnitude, demographic explanations are required.
problems.data_access: Leffler 2012 and Buffalo 2021 supplementary tables (open); GBIF via the organisms layer; recombination maps per species where published.

related_claims.label: Neutral equilibrium heterozygosity (Kimura-Crow)
Neutral theory: most molecular substitutions are neutral
Neutral substitution rate equals the mutation rate

approaches.title: Pre-registered phylogenetic test of three quantitative predictions for the π–N slope
approaches.method: Extend Buffalo's (2021) compilation with independent census proxies from the organisms layer and state, before analysis, the slope each hypothesis predicts. Response: log₁₀ π at synonymous or neutral sites. Census proxy: log₁₀(range area × density), where range area is the convex hull or alpha hull of cleaned GBIF occurrences and density is predicted from body mass by Damuth's allometry (D ∝ M^−0.75), as Buffalo did, but with GBIF-derived ranges to test robustness. Predictions: (H0, neutral) slope of log π on log N_c ≈ 1 if N_e ∝ N_c and μ is constant; (H1, linked selection) slope reduced by the factor predicted from each species' map length and coding density using a Corbett-Detig-style model of background selection plus sweeps, computed per species before looking at π; (H2, demographic) π tracks the harmonic mean of population size, so slope ≈ 1 against harmonic-mean N but much less against current N_c. Fit PGLS with Pagel's λ (phylolm) on an Open Tree of Life synthetic tree with time calibration. Decision rule: H1 closes the gap if the observed slope lies within the 95% interval of the H1-predicted slope; H0 is refuted if the slope interval excludes 0.5.
steps: Write result.json with predicted slopes and intervals for H0, H1 and H2 before computing observed slopes.
Resolve species through the organisms layer; fetch GBIF occurrences with a cleaning pipeline (coordinate checks, outlier removal) and compute ranges.
Compute per-species predicted linked-selection reduction from published map lengths and genome annotations; record n for which inputs exist.
Fit PGLS; compare slopes; report residual orders of magnitude unexplained.
approaches.decisive_result: Observed PGLS slope with 95% CI compared against the pre-registered H0 and H1 intervals: the gap is closed if the observed slope falls in the H1 interval, and the residual is quantified in orders of magnitude otherwise. The minimum sample is 100 species with π and range; Buffalo's set is larger, so recombination-map availability limits only the H1 subset.
approaches.failure_signature: Census proxies from GBIF ranges and Damuth density have measurement error so large (or so correlated with body mass) that slope intervals overlap all three predictions: inconclusive, underpowered.
approaches.missing: Recombination maps exist for a minority of species, so H1 can be tested only on a subset; census-size estimation remains crude.

approaches.title: Decompose π into N_e and μ using pedigree mutation rates
approaches.method: Part of the paradox may sit in μ, not N_e: the drift-barrier hypothesis predicts that per-generation mutation rate falls as N_e rises, which flattens π = 4N_eμ against N_c. Pedigree-based germline mutation rates now exist for dozens of vertebrates (Bergeron et al. 2023). For every species with both a pedigree μ and a published π (Romiguier et al. 2014, Leffler et al. 2012, genome-scale estimates in NCBI-linked studies), compute N̂_e = π/(4μ) and fit log N̂_e on log N_c (PGLS). Pre-registered predictions: if the paradox is entirely in N_e, then log μ is uncorrelated with log N_c and the slope of log N̂_e equals the slope of log π; if drift-barrier compression matters, log μ declines with log N_c and the N̂_e slope is steeper than the π slope by the μ slope. The quantity of interest is the fraction of the gap between neutral slope 1 and the observed π slope that μ accounts for.
steps: Pre-register the decomposition and predicted signs; list admissible μ estimates (trio-based, with stated callable-genome correction).
Assemble the matched set (species with both μ and π); resolve taxa via the organisms layer.
Fit PGLS for log π, log μ and log N̂_e on log N_c; propagate μ uncertainty by parametric bootstrap.
Report the share of the paradox attributable to μ with its 95% interval.
approaches.decisive_result: The estimated slope of log μ on log N_c and the implied share of the π–N_c gap explained by mutation-rate variation, with 95% CI. If the share's interval excludes 0, μ is a quantified part of the answer; if it is centred near 0 with a tight interval, the paradox is entirely in N_e.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than about 30 species with both pedigree μ and comparable π, giving intervals spanning 0 to 100%: inconclusive, underpowered.

approaches.title: Simulation bound on how much linked selection can flatten π across N
approaches.method: Settle whether linked selection can close the gap by computing the most it could do under generous but empirically bounded parameters. Use SLiM forward simulation with tree-sequence recording plus msprime recapitation, and stdpopsim genome models and DFEs where available, across a ladder of census sizes N from 10^3 to 10^7 simulated directly. Extrapolate to 10^12 with the analytic background-selection and sweep formulas (B = exp(−Σ u/(s(1+r/s)²)) plus a recurrent-sweep coalescent rate), calibrated against the simulations in the overlap range. Upper-bound parameters: the deleterious mutation rate at the top of published estimates, a DFE fraction of strongly selected new mutations at the top of estimates, and adaptive substitution rate α from McDonald–Kreitman ranges. Output: the curve π(N) and the maximum achievable flattening (slope of log π on log N over 10^4–10^12). Compare with the observed slope from approach 1 or from Buffalo 2021.
steps: Choose 3 representative genome architectures (vertebrate, insect, plant) from stdpopsim; fix parameter ranges from literature before simulating.
Run SLiM simulations over the N ladder with 20 replicates each; compute π at neutral sites.
Calibrate the analytic B and sweep model to simulations; extrapolate to large N.
Compute the maximum flattening and compare with the observed slope.
approaches.decisive_result: The minimum π–N slope achievable by linked selection under upper-bound parameters. If that minimum exceeds the observed slope plus its CI, linked selection cannot explain the paradox, as Buffalo argued, and demography or μ must; if it falls below, the bound shows which parameter regime is needed.
approaches.failure_signature: Extrapolation from 10^7 to 10^12 is unreliable: the analytic model misfits simulations at the top of the ladder, or sweep interference (genetic draft saturation) makes predictions model-dependent across plausible formulas.
approaches.missing: Direct simulation at N ≥ 10^8 is infeasible, so the bound rests on extrapolation.

approaches.title: Phylogenetic decomposition of diversity constraints
approaches.method: Pre-register a phylogenetic hierarchical model for autosomal synonymous diversity across at least 150 animal species. Predict log diversity from log census proxy, recombination-map length, functional genomic density, body size, range area from GBIF, and generation time, with clade random slopes and measurement error. Compare neutral, linked-selection and boom-bust models by leave-one-clade-out expected log predictive density.
steps: Freeze taxon inclusion, one diversity estimate per species and GBIF coverage rules before fitting.
Require at least 30 species with measured recombination maps and 150 total with range proxies.
Fit matched neutral, background-selection and recurrent-sweep models with a fixed phylogeny.
Report slope residuals, variance explained and held-out calibration.
approaches.decisive_result: Linked selection closes the gap only if its model improves leave-one-clade-out ELPD by at least 10 and leaves an absolute census-diversity slope residual below 0.05; otherwise the residual is quantitatively unresolved.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than 30 independent recombination landscapes or posterior predictions dominated by range-size measurement error make the mechanism comparison underpowered.
approaches.missing: Comparable recombination maps and defensible census sizes are sparse outside model organisms.

approaches.title: Genome-window test of linked-selection predictions
approaches.method: Within species, use genome windows to avoid uncertain census sizes. For at least 20 species with polymorphism, recombination and annotation data, preregister the reduction in neutral diversity near conserved or selected sites predicted by background-selection maps, then aggregate the measured maximum genome-wide reduction into a cross-species upper bound on how much linked selection can compress diversity.
steps: Select species and neutral-site filters without inspecting diversity-recombination associations.
Fit a common monotone recombination-diversity model with species-specific intercepts.
Cross-validate chromosome-held-out predictions and estimate diversity absent linked selection.
Regress corrected diversity on GBIF range and life-history proxies.
approaches.decisive_result: If linked selection explains at least 80% of within-genome neutral-diversity variance and corrected cross-species diversity spans under two orders of magnitude, it is sufficient for the tested taxa; a corrected span above three orders refutes sufficiency.
approaches.failure_signature: Neutral-site definitions or recombination maps are incomparable enough that chromosome-held-out prediction R2 is below 0.1 in more than half the species.
approaches.missing: Harmonized population-genomic callsets and recombination maps.

approaches.title: Pre-register the diversity-census slope with a range covariate
approaches.method: Pre-register before downloading tables. Response is log10 of nucleotide diversity π from the Leffler et al. 2012 compilation, with the Buffalo 2021 estimates used only as a second, separately reported column where the species overlap. Predictor is log10 of census size as published in those supplements. Covariate is log10 of GBIF range area: occurrences for the species with coordinate uncertainty below 10 km, reduced to presence on a 0.1 degree grid, range area the axis-aligned bounding box, species with fewer than 20 occupied cells dropped. Primary estimator is a nested taxonomic random-effects model, species within genus within family within order, fit by REML, not a single time-calibrated tree of all life. Neutral prediction is slope 1 of log10 π on log10 N. Secondary estimator, mammals only, is PGLS with Pagel's lambda on 100 trees from the Upham, Esselstyn and Jetz credible set. Linked selection is not fit in this approach. The verdict is about the slope: if the 95 percent profile interval includes 1, neutral scaling of diversity with census size is not rejected and the paradox sits in the intercept.
steps: Write the model, the GBIF filter and the drop rule before opening the supplements.
Join Leffler diversity and census size to GBIF bounding-box area.
Fit the nested random-effects model by REML and record the profile interval for the slope.
Repeat PGLS on the mammal overlap across 100 Upham trees.
Call the estimators mixed if one interval contains 1 and the other excludes it.
approaches.decisive_result: A 95 percent interval for the slope of log10 π on log10 census N. Neutral scaling is rejected only if that interval excludes 1 in the primary model.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than 30 species survive the GBIF cell filter, in which case the verdict is inconclusive and underpowered. A slope interval that includes both 0 and 1 is also indecisive and is reported as such.
approaches.missing: Census sizes are only as good as the supplements. GBIF bounding boxes are a range proxy, not a census, and the model treats them as a covariate rather than as N.

approaches.title: Test whether published recombination maps close the residual
approaches.method: Pre-register a second test aimed at linked selection, using only species that have both a diversity estimate in the Leffler or Buffalo tables and a public genetic map with at least 10^3 markers in centimorgans. Homo sapiens enters through the 1000 Genomes resource; every other species enters only with a map meeting the same marker floor. For each such species compute map length per megabase. Fit log10 π = a + b log10 N + c (map length per megabase) in the same nested taxonomic model as the slope test. Linked selection closes the gap only if, after this covariate, the residual slope on log10 N has a 95 percent interval containing 0 and the root-mean-square residual of log10 π is below 0.5. Both conditions are required. If fewer than 8 species qualify, the verdict is inconclusive, underpowered, and is not filled in by dropping the marker floor.
steps: Freeze the marker floor and the two numerical conditions before listing species.
Admit a species only when both a diversity row and a qualifying public map exist.
Fit the nested model with map length per megabase as covariate.
Record the residual slope interval and the residual RMSE.
Stop as underpowered if fewer than 8 species qualify.
approaches.decisive_result: Residual slope interval containing 0 and residual RMSE of log10 π below 0.5, on at least 8 species with real maps. Otherwise linked selection, as measured here, does not close the gap.
approaches.failure_signature: The residual slope interval excludes 0, or the RMSE stays at or above 0.5. Dropping the marker floor after seeing the fit is a failed pre-registration, not a result.
approaches.missing: Public genetic maps for most of the Leffler species. The test is designed to return underpowered rather than to invent maps.

approaches.title: Forward simulations of sweeps, background selection and bottlenecks
approaches.method: Ask whether a pre-specified demographic-plus-selection process can reproduce the empirical slope, using the slope from the first approach as a fixed target and not refitting it. Three regimes, parameters frozen first: neutral Wright–Fisher with N_e equal to census N; recurrent hitchhiking plus background selection with a stated deleterious mutation rate and a beneficial rate scaled per megabase; and a bottleneck regime with a contraction of factor 100 lasting a stated fraction of each run. For each regime, simulate a grid of census sizes spanning the empirical range, 20 replicates per size, and estimate the slope of mean log10 π on log10 N. A regime accounts for the paradox only if its slope's simulation interval covers the empirical slope and its diversity range covers the empirical diversity range within a factor of two at both ends. Code and seeds are part of the result.
steps: Freeze mutation rates, selection coefficients and the bottleneck schedule before fitting.
Simulate the three regimes across the census-size grid, 20 replicates.
Estimate each regime's slope of log10 π on log10 N.
Compare slope and endpoint diversity with the empirical target.
Reject a regime that misses either the slope or the endpoint range.
approaches.decisive_result: A regime whose simulated slope interval covers the empirical slope and whose diversity range matches both empirical endpoints within a factor of two. If none does, demography-plus-linked-selection of this form does not resolve the paradox.
approaches.failure_signature: All three regimes miss the slope or the endpoint range. Tuning the rates after seeing the empirical slope is a failed pre-registration.
approaches.missing: Species-specific recombination maps are not used here; the regimes are deliberately generic. A species-matched map is the other approach.

problems.title: Is there a universal metabolic scaling exponent?
problems.question: Does basal metabolic rate scale with body mass with a single exponent across taxa, and if so is it 3/4 (fractal supply networks) or 2/3 (surface-to-volume), or does the exponent vary systematically with taxon, temperature and body size?
problems.known_state: Kleiber (1932) reported 3/4; West, Brown and Enquist (1997) derived 3/4 from space-filling branching networks; White and Seymour (2003) found 2/3 for mammals once body temperature and digestive state are controlled; Kozlowski and Konarzewski (2004) disputed the WBE derivation. Current syntheses find curvature and taxon dependence. Thompson's surface-volume claims (ch02-01, ch03-07) encode the 2/3 alternative.
acceptance_criteria: A pre-registered phylogenetically controlled analysis across the organism taxa with AnAge/PanTHERIA body mass and metabolic data, with stated predictions: a single exponent with 95% interval excluding one of 2/3 and 3/4, or a model-comparison verdict that a curved or taxon-specific model beats any single power law.
A Lean 4 formalization of the WBE derivation stating its assumptions as hypotheses, so the disputed step is explicit.
falsifiers: If the pooled exponent interval contains both 2/3 and 3/4 after controls, the universality question is empirically underdetermined with present data.
problems.data_access: AnAge (open), PanTHERIA (open), White and Seymour 2003 compilation; taxon resolution via test-data/organisms.

related_claims.label: Weight tends to vary as the cube of linear dimensions during growth
Changes in the length-weight constant k reveal changes of form during growth
Cold-blooded animals approach a maximal size only asymptotically

approaches.title: Pre-registered PGLS model comparison: single power law vs curvature vs clade slopes
approaches.method: Assemble mammal BMR and mass from AnAge (metabolic rate, body mass, body temperature fields) and PanTHERIA (BasalMetRate, AdultBodyMass), deduplicated by species via the organisms layer. Exclude records not meeting basal criteria where flagged, and require n ≥ 300 species with temperature for the temperature-corrected analysis. Phylogeny: Upham et al. 2019 node-dated mammal trees, with analyses integrated over 100 posterior trees. Models: (M1) log B = a + b log M; (M2) M1 + Boltzmann temperature term −E/(kT_b) (Gillooly form) or T_b as covariate; (M3) quadratic in log M (Kolokotrones curvature); (M4) order-level random slopes. Fit by PGLS with Pagel's λ, compare by AICc and by leave-one-order-out predictive log-likelihood. Pre-registered decision: 'single exponent' if M1 or M2 wins and the 95% CI of b excludes one of 2/3 or 3/4 (reported as such); 'no universal exponent' if M3 or M4 improves predictive log-likelihood by > 10 units summed over orders; 'underdetermined' if the CI contains both.
steps: Write result.json with models, decision rule and minimum n before downloading.
Download AnAge (dataset.zip) and PanTHERIA; record SHA-256; merge and resolve taxa.
Prune Upham trees to the matched species; fit M1–M4 over 100 trees.
Report b with CI, curvature coefficient, order-slope variance and the verdict.
approaches.decisive_result: A verdict among 'exponent b with CI excluding 2/3 (or 3/4)', 'curved or clade-specific model wins by > 10 log-likelihood units out of sample', or 'underdetermined', with effect sizes. Mammals alone give n of several hundred species, enough to separate 2/3 from 3/4 if the relation is linear (White and Seymour's CI was about ±0.03).
approaches.failure_signature: Strong dependence of b on inclusion criteria (basal versus resting, captive versus wild) that the pre-registered criteria cannot resolve; the verdict then rests on data curation rather than biology.

approaches.title: Lean formalization of the WBE network derivation with the finite-size exponent
approaches.method: Make the disputed step explicit. Model: a branching network with N levels, branching ratio n, radius ratio β and length ratio γ per level, invariant terminal units (capillaries) and total blood volume V_b ∝ M. Define V_b(N) = Σ_{k=0}^{N} n^k π r_k² l_k with r_k = β^k r₀, l_k = γ^k l₀, so V_b = π r₀² l₀ Σ (nβ²γ)^k. Theorem 1 (exact finite form): with terminal size fixed, N_cap = n^N and V_b = V_cap · ((nβ²γ)^{−(N+1)} − 1)/((nβ²γ)^{−1} − 1) for nβ²γ < 1. Theorem 2 (asymptotic exponent): under area preservation β = n^{−1/2} and space filling γ = n^{−1/3}, and V_b ∝ M, the ratio log N_cap / log M → 3/4 as N → ∞, but for finite N the effective exponent is strictly less than 3/4 with an explicit correction term, matching Savage et al. 2008's finite-size analysis. Theorem 3: if area-preserving branching holds only below a transition level and Poiseuille scaling (β = n^{−1/3}) above it, the limiting exponent is different (explicit formula). The hypotheses V_b ∝ M and invariant terminal units are exactly where Kozłowski and Konarzewski object, and they appear as named hypotheses.
steps: Define the network sums in Lean (Finset.sum over levels, geometric series).
Prove Theorem 1 by geometric-series lemmas, and Theorem 2 by limits (Filter.Tendsto) on logarithms.
Prove Theorem 3 for the two-regime network.
Write a report with each hypothesis named and linked to Thompson's ch03-07 and ch02-01 claims; state which are empirical.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean module proving that WBE's 3/4 is the N → ∞ limit under four named hypotheses, with the exact finite-N exponent, compiled with only standard axioms. Each published objection then corresponds to dropping a named hypothesis.
approaches.failure_signature: The formalization shows that the published derivation needs a hypothesis not listed (for example a specific relation between N and M) to get 3/4, which is a substantive finding about WBE rather than a failure, or the limit proofs in Mathlib take longer than budgeted.

approaches.title: Cross-domain heterogeneity test: one exponent across prokaryotes, protists and animals?
approaches.method: Universality claims cover all life, but approach 1 tests mammals. DeLong et al. 2010 compiled metabolic rates for prokaryotes, protists and metazoans and reported superlinear, approximately linear and sublinear exponents respectively. Re-analyse with a pre-registered hierarchical model: log B = a_g + b_g log M + temperature correction, with group g ∈ {prokaryotes, protists, ectothermic metazoans, endotherms}, b_g ~ Normal(b̄, τ²). Pre-registered decision: universality is refuted if τ's 95% posterior interval excludes 0.05 and at least two b_g intervals are disjoint; supported if τ < 0.03 and b̄'s interval contains 3/4 or 2/3. Add AnAge ectotherm entries with temperature to test whether temperature correction collapses ectotherm and endotherm slopes, as metabolic theory predicts.
steps: Pre-register the model, priors and decision thresholds.
Retrieve DeLong et al. 2010 supplementary data; add AnAge ectotherm records with temperature.
Fit the hierarchical model (Stan or PyMC) with measurement-error terms on M where reported.
Report τ, group slopes and the verdict; check sensitivity to the temperature correction.
approaches.decisive_result: The posterior for between-group slope heterogeneity τ, and whether group slopes overlap. Disjoint slopes across domains refute a single universal exponent regardless of the mammal result.
approaches.failure_signature: Group samples (especially prokaryotes and protists) too small or too heterogeneous in measurement protocol for slopes to be compared, leaving τ's interval wide: inconclusive, underpowered.

approaches.title: Phylogenetic model comparison across endotherms
approaches.method: Pre-register adult, postabsorptive, thermoneutral basal-metabolism inclusion rules and fit mammal and bird data with phylogenetic generalized least squares. Compare fixed slopes 2/3 and 3/4, an estimated common slope, clade-specific slopes and a quadratic log-mass model using leave-one-family-out prediction.
steps: Resolve taxa against the organisms layer and deduplicate measurements by source.
Require at least 300 species and 20 families, recording temperature and measurement protocol.
Fit all five models with body-temperature and study random effects.
Use family-held-out ELPD and calibrated residuals for the preregistered verdict.
approaches.decisive_result: Universality is supported only if one common-slope model beats every curved or clade-varying model by ELPD at least 10 and its 95% interval width is below 0.04; otherwise report the best heterogeneity structure.
approaches.failure_signature: Protocol covariates are missing for over 30% of records or 2/3 and 3/4 remain inside the common-slope interval, yielding an inconclusive universal exponent.

approaches.title: Formal audit of the WBE exponent derivation
approaches.method: Encode an idealized branching network with branch ratio, length ratio, radius ratio, terminal-unit invariance and space-filling assumptions. Prove each exponent implication separately in Lean, including where area preservation or impedance minimization enters, and construct countermodels when assumptions are weakened.
steps: Represent finite self-similar trees and derive total serviced volume and network volume.
Prove logarithmic exponent lemmas with positivity and nondegeneracy hypotheses.
Derive 3/4 only from a named minimal assumption set.
Use exact finite trees to exhibit assumption-compatible alternatives producing 2/3 or other exponents.
approaches.decisive_result: A no-sorry theorem stating the minimal explicit hypotheses implying exponent 3/4, plus checked countermodels showing which omitted hypotheses destroy the conclusion.
approaches.failure_signature: The biological assumptions cannot be stated without directly assuming the desired scaling relation, showing that the derivation has no independent formal content.
approaches.missing: Formalization settles logical validity, not whether organisms satisfy the assumptions.

approaches.title: PGLS of PanTHERIA basal rate against body mass
approaches.method: Use PanTHERIA 1.0, Wilson and Reeder 2005 file, columns 18-1_BasalMetRate_mLO2hr and the paired mass 5-2_BasalMetRateMass_g. The Ecological Archives metadata says metabolic rate was accepted only with a mass from the same individuals, measured resting, post-absorptive, in the thermoneutral zone. Drop the missing-value code -999. Primary regression is log10(BMR) on log10(paired mass), PGLS with Pagel's lambda, repeated on 100 trees from the Upham credible set. A species-typical mass sensitivity uses 5-1_AdultBodyMass_g and is reported separately. Model comparison, pre-registered: a single slope, order-specific slopes, and a quadratic term in log mass. The curved or order-specific model wins if its AIC beats the single power law by more than 10 on at least 95 of the 100 trees. The single-exponent claim is decided by the 95 percent interval of the single slope: it must exclude either 2/3 or 3/4. If the interval contains both, the question is underdetermined, which is the problem's own falsifier. Geographic mean temperature in PanTHERIA is not body temperature and is not used as a thermoregulatory control.
steps: Pre-register the columns, the missing code, the AIC gap and the two target exponents.
Drop -999 and match species to the Upham trees.
Fit Pagel's lambda PGLS on 100 trees for the paired-mass regression.
Compare single-slope, order-specific and quadratic models by AIC.
Repeat with adult body mass as a labeled sensitivity and do not pool the two masses.
approaches.decisive_result: On at least 95 of 100 trees, either a single-slope 95 percent interval that excludes 2/3 or excludes 3/4, or an order-specific or quadratic model that beats the power law by AIC of more than 10.
approaches.failure_signature: The single-slope interval contains both 2/3 and 3/4 and no alternative model beats the power law by the AIC gap. The universality question is then underdetermined on PanTHERIA.
approaches.missing: A species-level body-temperature table joined to this taxonomy. PanTHERIA's geographic temperature is not a substitute, so the White and Seymour control is not replicated here.

approaches.title: Lean statement of the West–Brown–Enquist exponent
approaches.method: Formalize the scaling argument under explicit hypotheses, and make the step Kozlowski and Konarzewski dispute a separate lemma. Hypotheses: a self-similar branching network with fixed branching ratio; a space-filling condition relating the linear scale factor to that ratio; a terminal unit whose size does not depend on body mass; and a flow or impedance condition that fixes how cross-section scales across a branch. From those, prove that metabolic rate scales as mass to the 3/4. Then prove a second lemma that names the alternative service-volume assumption used in the critique and shows whether it is consistent with invariant terminal units. The module must not hide either assumption inside a definition. Empirical truth of the hypotheses is out of scope, as in the Thompson Lean standard.
steps: Define branching ratio, scale factor, terminal-unit size and service volume.
Prove the 3/4 exponent from the stated hypotheses.
State the critiqued service-volume assumption as a second definition.
Prove consistency or inconsistency with invariant terminal units.
Audit axioms and write the scope note that the hypotheses are not data.
approaches.decisive_result: A no-sorry derivation of the 3/4 exponent under named hypotheses, and a second lemma that settles consistency of the critiqued alternative with invariant capillaries.
approaches.failure_signature: The 3/4 exponent is obtained only by assuming the conclusion, or the two lemmas use incompatible definitions of service volume without saying so.

approaches.title: Finite-generation networks and the approach to 3/4
approaches.method: The Lean theorem is an infinite-generation statement. Build the finite network the hypotheses describe: branching ratio 2, generations G from 2 to 24, area-preserving branch radii, terminal units of fixed size, service volume the sum of the terminal service volumes. Define metabolic rate as total terminal flow. Regress log rate on log service volume across the generation sequence and report the local exponent between successive generations. The numerical claim matching the theorem is that the local exponent is within 0.01 of 3/4 by some G at most 24. Also build the alternative network from the critique's service-volume assumption and report its exponent. This checks the algebra of both lemmas and says nothing about real mammals.
steps: Implement both finite networks from the Lean hypotheses.
Compute total flow and service volume at each generation from 2 to 24.
Estimate the local log-log exponent between successive generations.
Test whether the primary network is within 0.01 of 3/4 by generation 24.
Report the alternative network's exponent beside it.
approaches.decisive_result: The primary network's local exponent lies within 0.01 of 3/4 at some generation at most 24, and the alternative network's exponent is reported from the same code.
approaches.failure_signature: The primary exponent stays more than 0.01 away from 3/4 through generation 24. The finite network then does not realize the theorem, and one of the two must be wrong.
